title: Principal-Agent
subtitle: Moral Hazard & Incentive Contracts
concept: The Principal-Agent problem arises when one party (the agent) acts on behalf of another (the principal), but the principal cannot directly observe the agent's actions. Because effort is hidden, the agent may under-perform — this is called moral hazard. The principal's challenge is to design a contract that aligns the agent's self-interest with the principal's goals.
setup: You are the agent (employee). The principal (employer) offers you a fixed wage plus a bonus if the outcome is successful. Each round you secretly choose: High Effort (higher success probability, but costs you something) or Low Effort (lower success probability, but free). The principal only sees whether the outcome was a success or failure — not which effort level you chose.
keyInsight: A well-designed incentive contract can align the agent's private interests with the principal's goals — making high effort the rational choice. But because effort is unobservable, some agents will still shirk, and that is exactly the moral hazard the contract is designed to prevent.
lessons: Without a bonus, agents would always choose Low Effort — it gives the same wage with no cost. Fixed wages alone cannot solve moral hazard.

The success bonus is calibrated so that High Effort yields a higher expected payoff than Low Effort. This is called an incentive-compatible contract — it makes doing the right thing personally rational.
Even with the right contract, some agents still choose Low Effort, hoping to get lucky. This is moral hazard in action — you can see it in the class results.
The principal can never be sure whether a bad outcome was bad luck or low effort. This ambiguity is the fundamental challenge of hidden-action problems.

strategies.name: Always High Effort
strategies.outcome: Maximises your expected payoff over the game. With default config: $10 wage + $50×0.8 bonus − $20 cost = $30 expected per round vs. $10 + $50×0.3 − $0 = $25 for Low. High effort earns $5 more per round on average — about $25 extra over 5 rounds.
strategies.insight: This is what the contract was designed to induce. You are behaving as the principal intended, and you are rewarded for it in expectation.

strategies.name: Always Low Effort
strategies.outcome: Saves the effort cost every round but earns less on average. You score $25 expected instead of $30 — a $5/round shortfall. Over 5 rounds you fall roughly $25 behind High Effort players.
strategies.insight: This is moral hazard: exploiting the fact that the principal cannot observe your effort. Rational in the very short run, self-defeating over the full game.

strategies.name: Mixed / Opportunistic
strategies.outcome: Unpredictable results. Some rounds you benefit from saving the cost; others you lose big on low-probability outcomes. Your score is unlikely to beat a consistent High Effort strategy.
strategies.insight: Illustrates why employers in the real world use monitoring, probationary periods, vesting schedules, and repeated relationships — to sustain effort over time.

classroomObservations: Watch the round-by-round results panel: you will almost always see a mix of High and Low effort choices, even though High dominates in expectation. This is the point — even with a well-designed contract, moral hazard persists. Ask students: if they chose Low Effort, why? If the class was told effort would be revealed at the end, would choices change? That thought experiment isolates the role of observability.
realWorld: CEO performance bonuses are calibrated to make high effort rational. Insurance deductibles make risky behaviour costly for the insured. Sales commissions align rep effort with firm revenue. Doctor fee-for-service models (pay per procedure) can create the opposite problem — incentivising over-treatment. The structure of the contract determines everything.
tip: The expected payoff formula is: wage + bonus × success_probability − effort_cost. Plug in both effort levels and compare — High Effort should come out ahead with the default config. If it doesn't, the contract is broken.
furtherReading: Jensen & Meckling (1976) — Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behaviour, Agency Costs and Ownership Structure; Holmstrom (1979) — Moral Hazard and Observability; Mirrlees (1999) — The Theory of Moral Hazard and Unobservable Behaviour
numericalExample: With default config (wage=$10, bonus=$50, pH=0.8, pL=0.3, effort cost=$20): High Effort expected payoff = $10 + $50×0.8 − $20 = $30 per round. Low Effort = $10 + $50×0.3 − $0 = $25 per round. Over 5 rounds, always-High earns ~$150 expected vs ~$125 for always-Low — a $25 gap. But because outcomes are probabilistic, a Low-effort player who gets lucky can outscore a High-effort player in any single round.

title: Signaling Game
subtitle: Spence Education Signaling
concept: Workers know their own productivity (their 'type') but employers do not. This information asymmetry means employers cannot pay workers their true marginal product. Education can solve this — not because it necessarily makes workers more productive, but because it is cheaper for high-productivity workers to acquire. This cost difference is what makes education a credible signal.
setup: You are randomly assigned a worker type — High or Low — which you know but your employer does not. Each round you choose an education level (0, 1, or 2). The employer pays a wage based only on your education choice. Your payoff is the wage minus the cost of education, which depends on your type. High types have a lower cost per education level than Low types.
keyInsight: In a separating equilibrium, High types choose full education (edu=2) and Low types choose no education (edu=0). The signal is credible precisely because Low types find it too expensive to imitate. Education separates types not because it teaches skills, but because of its differential cost.
lessons: The key condition for a separating equilibrium: the wage premium for high education must exceed the signalling cost for High types, but NOT for Low types. If this holds, only High types will signal.
Education can have pure signalling value even if it adds zero productive skill. Spence's model is deliberately extreme — but it captures something real about credentials and positional competition.

If the wage premium is too small, or costs are too similar across types, a pooling equilibrium emerges: everyone chooses the same education level and types are indistinguishable. The market fails to sort.
Watch whether the class separates over multiple rounds. If High types consistently choose edu=2 and Low types choose edu=0, a separating equilibrium has emerged from decentralised decisions.

strategies.name: High-type: choose edu=2 (Full)
strategies.outcome: Earns the high wage ($100) with cost $20 (2 levels × $10), netting $80. If Low types don't follow, this credibly identifies you as High type. The equilibrium strategy.
strategies.insight: The signal works because Low types face cost $80 (2 × $40) for edu=2, netting only $20 — not worth it. High types can afford to signal; Low types cannot.

strategies.name: Low-type: choose edu=0 (None)
strategies.outcome: Earns the baseline wage ($50) with zero cost — net $50. Trying to mimic (edu=2) would cost $80 and yield $100 − $80 = $20. Worse than staying at edu=0.
strategies.insight: Self-selection at work: the cost structure makes honest revelation personally optimal. No enforcement needed — the signal is self-sorting.

strategies.name: Everyone pools at edu=0
strategies.outcome: All earn the pooling wage (average of High and Low types). High types are underpaid; Low types are overpaid. No information is conveyed. This is the outcome with no signalling.
strategies.insight: Pooling equilibria are also valid game-theoretic outcomes. Whether separation or pooling emerges depends on the wage schedule and cost parameters — change them in the host settings to explore.

classroomObservations: Does separation emerge? In the first round, players often experiment. By round 3-4, High types typically converge on edu=2 and Low types on edu=0 — the separating equilibrium appears spontaneously without coordination. Ask students: does this mean education is 'just' signalling? That is the debate that has raged since Spence (1973).
realWorld: University degrees, professional certifications (CFA, bar exams), unpaid internships, military service, and even luxury goods can function as Spence signals. The question to ask is always: is this qualification making you more productive, or is it just separating you from people who wouldn't do it?
tip: Your type is shown in the info bar during the game. Use it to calculate your net payoff for each education level before choosing. The table in the 'How It Works' card updates with the current round's wage schedule.
furtherReading: Spence (1973) — Job Market Signaling (Nobel Prize 2001); Riley (2001) — Silver Signals: Twenty-Five Years of Screening and Signaling; Weiss (1995) — Human Capital vs. Signalling Explanations of Wages
numericalExample: Default config: High-type cost=$10/level, Low-type cost=$40/level. Wages: edu=0->$50, edu=1->$50, edu=2->$100. High type at edu=2 nets $100-20=$80. Low type mimicking edu=2 nets $100-80=$20, far worse than staying at edu=0 for $50. That $30 gap is what makes the signal self-enforcing.

title: Adverse Selection
subtitle: Market for Lemons & Information Asymmetry
concept: When buyers and sellers have different information about quality, markets can break down. Sellers know the quality of what they are selling; buyers do not. Buyers therefore only pay the average price — which drives out high-quality sellers, who can't get a fair price. This lowers average quality, which lowers prices further, which drives out more high-quality sellers. The market unravels.
setup: Players act as buyers and sellers in a market with hidden quality. Sellers know whether their goods are high or low quality; buyers only learn the average quality the market produces. The equilibrium price reflects average quality — which changes as sellers enter and exit. Watch whether high-quality goods disappear over time.
keyInsight: Information asymmetry can destroy markets entirely, even when trades would be mutually beneficial. The market does not just produce wrong prices — it may cease to exist. This is Akerlof's 'lemons problem': bad products drive good products out of the market.
lessons: The root cause is unverifiable quality: buyers cannot tell a lemon from a peach before buying. If they could, high-quality sellers would get fair prices and the market would function normally.

The unravelling process is a cascade: fewer good products → lower average quality → lower average price → even fewer good products. Each step is individually rational; the collective result is market failure.

Institutions that solve adverse selection work by making quality observable: warranties (signal quality), inspections (verify quality), reputation systems (track quality history), and third-party certification (vouch for quality).

Adverse selection in insurance is especially important: sicker people buy more coverage, so insurers face a pool that is sicker than the general population, which raises premiums, which drives out the healthiest, which raises premiums further.

strategies.name: Sell high-quality goods at pooling price
strategies.outcome: You are underpaid — you receive the average price when your goods are worth more. Rational to exit the market if the price falls far enough below your goods' value.
strategies.insight: This is the mechanism: high-quality sellers exit when they can't get a fair price, which worsens average quality for buyers.

strategies.name: Sell low-quality goods at pooling price
strategies.outcome: You are overpaid — you receive the average price when your goods are worth less. You profit from the information asymmetry.
strategies.insight: The perverse result: bad sellers benefit while good sellers are harmed. The market rewards dishonesty in the absence of verification.

strategies.name: Offer a warranty
strategies.outcome: Signals high quality credibly. Expensive for low-quality sellers to offer (they'd face many claims), cheap for high-quality sellers. Buyers accept the warranty as proof of quality and pay a premium.
strategies.insight: Warranties are a separating signal — the same logic as Spence's education model but in a product market.

classroomObservations: Track the average quality traded across rounds — you should see it decline as high-quality sellers exit. Point out to students that this is not fraud: everyone is acting rationally. The market failure arises from the structure of information, not from dishonesty.
realWorld: Used-car markets (the original Akerlof example), health insurance before the ACA mandate, mortgage-backed securities in 2007 (investors couldn't assess underlying loan quality), and labour markets (employers can't observe worker quality at hiring) all exhibit adverse selection. Carfax, MOT certificates, and Trustpilot reviews are market solutions.
tip: The solution to adverse selection always involves making hidden information visible — either by the informed party signalling quality or the uninformed party screening for it.
furtherReading: Akerlof (1970) — The Market for Lemons (Nobel Prize 2001); Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976) — Equilibrium in Competitive Insurance Markets; Stiglitz (2002) — Information and the Change in the Paradigm in Economics
numericalExample: Example: cars are worth $10,000 (high quality) or $2,000 (low quality), equally split. Buyers pay the average = $6,000. High-quality owners (who value them at $10,000) won't sell at $6,000 and exit. Now only low-quality remain. Buyers learn this and pay $2,000. Market shrinks from 100% of cars traded to 50%, destroying $4,000 of value per high-quality car that goes untraded.

title: Prisoner's Dilemma
subtitle: Cooperation vs. Defection
concept: Two players each choose to cooperate or defect. Mutual cooperation produces the best collective outcome, but each player has a dominant strategy to defect — regardless of what the other does. The result is mutual defection, which is worse for everyone. This is the central paradox of non-cooperative game theory.
setup: Each round you and your opponent simultaneously choose Cooperate or Defect. If both cooperate, you both earn a medium-high payoff. If both defect, you both earn a low payoff. If one cooperates and the other defects, the defector earns the highest payoff and the cooperator earns the lowest. You cannot communicate before choosing.
keyInsight: Individually rational choices produce collectively irrational outcomes. Defection is dominant — always better for you regardless of your opponent's choice — yet mutual defection is worse for both players than mutual cooperation. This gap between individual and collective rationality is the core tension in economics, politics, and everyday life.
lessons: Defection is a dominant strategy: it pays better whether your opponent cooperates or defects. Knowing this, both players defect — and both are worse off than if they had both cooperated. This is the Nash equilibrium.

In a one-shot game, there is no rational basis for cooperation. The prisoner's dilemma is 'solved' only by changing the game: repeated interaction, communication, binding commitments, or punishment mechanisms.

In repeated games (multiple rounds), cooperation can emerge through reciprocal strategies. Tit-for-Tat — cooperate first, then copy your opponent's last move — won Axelrod's famous tournament. It is nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and clear.

Real-world cooperation often works through reputation: if everyone knows you defected yesterday, they'll defect against you today. This converts the one-shot game into a repeated game with long-run consequences.

strategies.name: Always Defect
strategies.outcome: The Nash equilibrium of the one-shot game. You can never do worse by defecting than by cooperating, given what your opponent plays. But mutual defection gives both players the bad outcome.
strategies.insight: Dominance and collective optimality point in opposite directions. This is the dilemma.

strategies.name: Always Cooperate
strategies.outcome: Achieves the best collective outcome if both players cooperate. Completely exploitable — a permanent defector beats you every round.
strategies.insight: Cooperation requires trust and reciprocity. Without enforcement or reputation, unconditional cooperation is strategically naive.

strategies.name: Tit-for-Tat
strategies.outcome: Cooperate in round 1. From round 2 onwards, copy what your opponent did last round. Sustains mutual cooperation with cooperative opponents; punishes defectors immediately; forgives after one retaliatory defection.
strategies.insight: The most robust strategy in repeated prisoner's dilemma experiments. Its success shows that cooperation is evolutionarily stable when interactions repeat.

classroomObservations: Cooperation rates typically start around 40-60% and decline over rounds as players learn defection is safe. Point this out — it mirrors real-world trust erosion. Then ask: what would change cooperation rates? Shorter game length? Anonymous play? Public commitment? These variations illuminate the mechanisms behind cooperation.
realWorld: Price wars between oligopolists, arms races between nations, carbon emission agreements, competing firms choosing whether to advertise, and even two cafes deciding whether to stay open on Sundays all have prisoner's dilemma structure. OPEC struggles to sustain cooperation because members have incentives to over-produce.
tip: In the last round, there's no future to protect — rational players defect. Work backwards: if you'll defect in the last round, your opponent expects that and defects in round n-1, and so on. This 'backward induction' unravels cooperation in finite games.
furtherReading: Nash (1950) — Equilibrium Points in N-Person Games; Axelrod (1984) — The Evolution of Cooperation; Fudenberg & Maskin (1986) — The Folk Theorem in Repeated Games
numericalExample: Typical payoffs: Mutual cooperate = (3,3), Mutual defect = (1,1), One defects/one cooperates = (5,0). Defecting earns 5 vs 3 when opponent cooperates, and 1 vs 0 when opponent defects — defecting is always better by 2 points regardless of what the opponent does. Yet both players defecting (1,1) is worse than both cooperating (3,3) for everyone.

title: Public Goods
subtitle: Free Rider Problem & Collective Action
concept: Public goods are non-excludable (you can't stop people benefiting) and non-rival (one person's consumption doesn't reduce others'). These properties create the free-rider problem: each individual has an incentive to let others pay and enjoy the good for free. Private markets systematically under-provide public goods.
setup: Each round every player decides how much of their budget to contribute to a shared pool. Contributions are multiplied by a factor greater than 1 (reflecting the social return to public goods) and divided equally among all players, regardless of who contributed. Players who contribute nothing receive the same share of the pool as those who gave everything.
keyInsight: The Nash equilibrium is zero contribution — every player's best response is to free-ride. But if everyone free-rides, the public good is not provided and everyone is worse off. The socially optimal outcome (full contribution) requires either coercion (taxation) or norms that override individual incentives.
lessons: The free-rider problem is not a failure of morality — it is a logical consequence of non-excludability. Even people who want the public good to exist have an incentive to let others pay for it.

Contributions typically start around 40-60% of endowment and decline over rounds as players realise they are being free-ridden. This 'contribution decay' is one of the most replicated findings in experimental economics.

Conditional cooperation is the dominant behaviour: people contribute if others do, but punish free-riders by reducing their own contributions. This explains why public goods provision is fragile — it only takes a few free-riders to collapse cooperation.
Solutions: taxation (compulsory contribution), privatisation (excludable goods), Ostrom-style community governance (peer monitoring and sanctions), and social norms (shame and reciprocity).

strategies.name: Contribute zero (full free-ride)
strategies.outcome: The dominant strategy in a one-shot game. You pocket your full endowment and collect a share of everyone else's contributions. But if everyone does this, the pool is empty and everyone earns nothing from the public good.
strategies.insight: Individually rational, collectively disastrous. The tragedy of the public goods game.

strategies.name: Contribute fully
strategies.outcome: Socially efficient if everyone cooperates — total payoff is maximised. You are heavily exploited if others free-ride, since you contribute everything and receive back only 1/n of the total.
strategies.insight: Altruistic or socially minded players contribute more, but their contributions are undermined by free-riders. This drives the contribution decay seen in experiments.

strategies.name: Contribute conditionally
strategies.outcome: Match the average contribution of the group. Sustains cooperation when most players cooperate, collapses quickly when free-riders appear. The most commonly observed behaviour.
strategies.insight: Conditional cooperation explains both why public goods are sometimes provided (when groups are cooperative) and why they often fail (when free-riders undermine trust).

classroomObservations: Watch contributions over rounds — the decay pattern is reliable. In the debrief, show the total group payoff under full cooperation vs. the Nash equilibrium. The gap is the cost of the free-rider problem. Ask: what would change behaviour? Adding a punishment option (where players can pay to reduce free-riders' payoffs) dramatically raises contribution rates in experiments.
realWorld: National defence, clean air and water, open-source software, basic scientific research, herd immunity from vaccination, and street lighting are all public goods. Governments solve the free-rider problem through mandatory taxation — you cannot opt out of paying for national defence even if you don't value it.
tip: The social multiplier (how much contributions are multiplied before redistribution) determines whether full cooperation beats full free-riding. If the multiplier divided by the number of players exceeds 1, cooperation is socially optimal — but free-riding is still individually rational.
furtherReading: Samuelson (1954) — The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure; Ostrom (1990) — Governing the Commons (Nobel Prize 2009); Fehr & Gächter (2000) — Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments
numericalExample: 4 players, $10 endowment each, multiplier=1.6, equal split. If all 4 contribute $10: pool=$40, x1.6=$64, each gets $16. Net gain: +$6 each. If you free-ride ($0) while others give $10: pool=$30, x1.6=$48, split 4 ways=$12 to you + keep $10 = $22 total. Others get $12. So free-riding earns $22 vs $16 — a $6 personal gain but $4 less for everyone else.

title: Trust Game
subtitle: Trust, Reciprocity & Social Preferences
concept: The trust game tests whether people trust strangers and whether that trust is reciprocated. Standard economic theory predicts no trust — the receiver has no incentive to return anything, so the sender sends nothing. In reality, significant amounts are sent and returned, revealing that people have social preferences (caring about fairness and reciprocity) that standard models miss.
setup: The sender receives a sum of money and decides how much (if any) to send to the receiver. Whatever is sent is multiplied (reflecting the gains from cooperation). The receiver then decides how much to send back. The sender's payoff depends on their own return and what they kept. The receiver's payoff is what they receive minus what they return.
keyInsight: People are not purely self-interested. The subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium — send nothing, return nothing — is wrong as a description of human behaviour. Most senders send substantial amounts, and most receivers return more than the minimum. This tells us that fairness, reciprocity, and social norms are real economic forces.
lessons: Backward induction predicts the sender sends nothing: the receiver has no incentive to return anything (any return reduces their payoff), so the sender anticipates this and keeps everything. This is the standard prediction — and it is consistently violated.
In practice, senders send 40-60% of their endowment on average, and receivers return about 30-50% of what they receive (often enough to leave the sender slightly ahead). Trust earns positive returns.

The multiplier is the key: it means total surplus is always higher when the sender trusts. Trust is socially efficient. The question is whether the receiver's reciprocity makes it individually rational too.
Repeated interactions sustain higher trust: reputation, relationships, and the shadow of the future all raise return rates. One-shot interactions with strangers show lower trust and lower returns.

strategies.name: Sender: send everything
strategies.outcome: Maximises the total surplus available (due to the multiplier). Requires trusting the receiver to return at least as much as you sent. Risky in theory, often successful in practice because receivers reciprocate.
strategies.insight: High trust, high risk. But the data show that receivers are more reciprocal than rational self-interest predicts — so this strategy often pays off.

strategies.name: Sender: send nothing
strategies.outcome: Safe — you keep your endowment and guarantee your minimum payoff. But you forgo the gains from cooperation. The subgame-perfect equilibrium that nobody follows.
strategies.insight: The 'rational' prediction fails because it ignores social preferences. In practice, sending nothing signals distrust and leaves value on the table.

strategies.name: Receiver: return a fair share (≈50%)
strategies.outcome: Sustains the sender's trust, enables high total payoffs for both, and is the modal behaviour in experiments. Driven by reciprocity — the receiver matches the sender's generosity.
strategies.insight: Reciprocity norms are powerful. Receivers who receive more tend to return more — not because they rationally calculate, but because unfairness feels costly.

classroomObservations: Compare the average amount sent and returned to the game-theoretic predictions. The gap is striking. Ask students: why did you trust? Why did you return? The answers reveal social preferences that standard models ignore. Try varying whether the interaction is anonymous — trust typically falls with anonymity, showing that reputation and observability matter.
realWorld: Business contracts rely on trust — legal enforcement is a substitute when trust is low but a complement when it is high. Financial markets, employment relationships, supply chains, and even casual transactions (giving a tip before the service is delivered) are trust games. Countries with higher social trust have lower transaction costs and higher long-run growth.
tip: The optimal strategy depends on your beliefs about the receiver's reciprocity. In a one-shot game with a stranger, the standard theory says send nothing — but the data say send something. The expected return on trust is positive in most populations.
furtherReading: Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe (1995) — Trust, Reciprocity, and Social History; Fehr & Gächter (2000) — Fairness and Retaliation; Guiso, Sapienza & Zingales (2006) — Does Culture Affect Economic Outcomes?
numericalExample: Sender has $10, multiplier=3x. If sender sends $10: receiver gets $30. If receiver returns $15 (50%), sender ends with $15 — better than the $10 they kept. Both gain: sender +$5, receiver +$15. If receiver keeps everything, sender gets $0 (loses $10). Nash prediction: send $0. Experimental average: send ~$5, return ~$3-4 — trust generates positive expected return.

title: Ultimatum Game
subtitle: Fairness, Bargaining & Costly Punishment
concept: The proposer offers a split of a fixed sum; the responder can accept or reject. If rejected, both get nothing. Standard theory predicts the proposer offers the minimum and the responder accepts (something is better than nothing). In reality, low offers are frequently rejected — people pay a real cost to punish unfairness.
setup: You are randomly assigned as proposer or responder. The proposer decides how to divide a fixed sum between themselves and the responder. The responder sees the offer and decides to accept or reject. If accepted, both receive the offered amounts. If rejected, both receive zero.
keyInsight: People have fairness preferences that override pure self-interest. Offers below roughly 30% of the total are rejected about half the time — responders sacrifice their own payoff to punish proposers they perceive as unfair. This 'costly punishment' is not predicted by standard models but is remarkably consistent across cultures and contexts.
lessons: Backward induction predicts: proposer offers $0.01, responder accepts (getting 1 cent is better than nothing). This prediction is wrong. Offers below 30% are typically rejected, and the modal offer is 40-50%.

Responders are not being irrational — they are expressing a preference for fairness. Rejecting an unfair offer is a credible punishment signal that disciplines future proposers. It can be rational in a population where others share the same preference.
Proposers know this: they offer more than self-interest would dictate because they anticipate rejection. The proposer is not being generous — they are being strategic about responder psychology.

Cultural variation exists but is bounded: rejection rates for low offers are high in all studied populations, but 'fairness thresholds' vary. Higher-income, more market-integrated societies tend to offer more equitable splits.

strategies.name: Proposer: offer 50/50
strategies.outcome: Almost never rejected. Leaves money on the table relative to the self-interest optimum, but is the safest strategy. Many proposers use this as a 'fairness anchor'.
strategies.insight: Equal splits are powerful norms. The 50/50 heuristic is cognitively simple and socially safe.

strategies.name: Proposer: offer 20-30%
strategies.outcome: Rejected roughly 40-60% of the time in experiments. Expected value may actually be lower than a 40% offer, depending on the group's rejection threshold.
strategies.insight: Greedy offers backfire. The proposer should model the responder's rejection probability as a function of offer size — the optimal offer is typically around 40-45%.

strategies.name: Responder: reject anything below 40%
strategies.outcome: You earn nothing when you reject, but you signal that exploitation has costs. In repeated settings, this disciplines proposers and raises the average offer you receive.
strategies.insight: Costly punishment is a commitment device. If proposers believe you will reject low offers, they offer more — your toughness benefits you over multiple interactions.

classroomObservations: Show the distribution of offers and rejection rates. Ask students who rejected: was it worth it? Economically, the answer depends on whether there are future interactions. Ask proposers who offered high amounts: were you being fair or strategic? Most will say both — which is the interesting finding.
realWorld: Labour negotiations, merger terms, divorce settlements, international trade deals, and tax policy all involve ultimatum-like bargaining. The finding that 'power without fairness invites costly resistance' is one of the most policy-relevant results in behavioural economics.
tip: If you are the proposer, think about what the responder considers 'fair'. The 50/50 offer is a Schelling point — both parties know it is fair, so it is a natural focal point for agreement.
furtherReading: Güth, Schmittberger & Schwarze (1982) — An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining; Thaler (1988) — The Ultimatum Game; Henrich et al. (2001) — In Search of Homo Economicus — cross-cultural ultimatum game evidence
numericalExample: Total pie = $10. Nash prediction: propose $0.01, accept (beats $0). Actual experimental results: modal offer = $4-5 (40-50%). Offers below $3 (30%) are rejected ~50% of the time. If proposer offers $2 and it gets rejected 50% of the time, expected payoff = 0.5 x $8 + 0.5 x $0 = $4. Compare to offering $4 (always accepted) = $6. The greedy proposer earns less in expectation.

title: Keynesian Beauty Contest
subtitle: Higher-Order Beliefs & Level-k Thinking
concept: Players guess a number between 0 and 100. The winner is whoever is closest to 2/3 of the average guess. The Nash equilibrium is 0 (if everyone reasons perfectly and knows everyone else does too). But real players use only a few levels of reasoning, and the winning guess depends on correctly modelling how deeply others think.
setup: Everyone simultaneously submits a number from 0 to 100. After all guesses are in, the average is calculated and multiplied by 2/3. The player closest to this target wins. There is no individual best strategy — your optimal guess depends on what you think others will guess, which depends on what they think you'll guess, and so on.
keyInsight: Rational play in strategic situations depends not on what you think is right, but on what you think others think. Keynes compared stock markets to a beauty contest where you win by picking the face others will pick — not the most beautiful face. This 'reflexive' structure means prices and markets are driven by higher-order beliefs, not just fundamentals.
lessons: Level-0 thinking: ignore strategy and guess randomly around 50. Level-1: assume others guess 50 and best-respond with 33. Level-2: assume others are Level-1 and guess 22. Level-k: iterate further down. Nash equilibrium (infinite levels) is 0.
Most first-time players submit guesses between 20 and 35, suggesting they use 1-2 levels of reasoning. This is one of the most stable findings in experimental economics.
The winning strategy is not the Nash equilibrium — it is one level above the average sophistication of your opponents. Guessing 0 loses to a class that mostly guesses 30.
Repeat the game immediately after revealing results. Guesses drop dramatically in round 2 as players update their beliefs about others' sophistication. By round 3, many classes converge close to 0.

strategies.name: Guess 33 (Level-1)
strategies.outcome: Best response to a group of Level-0 players (who average 50). Often wins in the first round of a class that hasn't played before.
strategies.insight: One level of strategic reasoning is enough to beat naive players — but loses to Level-2 thinkers.

strategies.name: Guess 22 (Level-2)
strategies.outcome: Best response to a group of Level-1 players. Wins when the class has learned from previous rounds. The most common 'sophisticated' first-round guess among economics students.
strategies.insight: Two levels of reasoning is approximately where real humans top out. Deeper reasoning has diminishing returns in populations that don't also reason deeply.

strategies.name: Guess 0 (Nash)
strategies.outcome: Theoretically correct but practically poor: you win only if everyone else also guesses 0. In any real group, the average will be well above 0 and you will lose by a large margin.
strategies.insight: This is the core insight: the Nash equilibrium is only correct when all players are rational AND all players know all players are rational AND everyone knows this. In reality, none of these hold.

classroomObservations: Reveal the average after round 1 and calculate 2/3 of it. Show the histogram of guesses. Ask students to explain their reasoning: most will describe 1-2 levels of thinking. Run round 2 immediately — the dramatic drop in guesses illustrates learning and updating. In round 3, ask: if everyone in this room is now guessing near 0, what should you guess?
realWorld: Stock prices are beauty contests — investors buy what they think others will buy tomorrow, not what they think is fundamentally valuable. This explains momentum effects, herding, and bubbles. Currency crises, viral content, and fashion trends all have this reflexive structure. Soros called this 'reflexivity'.
tip: Before guessing, think: what does the average person in this room think the average person will guess? Then take 2/3 of that. One level of reasoning above the room is usually enough to win.
furtherReading: Keynes (1936) — The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (Ch. 12); Nagel (1995) — Unraveling in Guessing Games: An Experimental Study; Ho, Camerer & Weigelt (1998) — Iterated Dominance and Iterated Best Response
numericalExample: Target = 2/3 of average. If average guess = 50, target = 33. If average = 33 (Level-1 room), target = 22. If average = 22, target = 15. Nash equilibrium = 0. In first-round experiments with general public, winning guesses are typically 22-28. With economics PhD students, winning guesses are 7-12. The class's sophistication determines the right answer.

title: Matching Pennies
subtitle: Zero-Sum Games & Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibria
concept: Each player simultaneously chooses Heads or Tails. One player wins if the choices match; the other wins if they differ. There is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium — any predictable strategy can be exploited. Both players must randomise to prevent the other from reading their strategy.
setup: Each round you and your opponent simultaneously choose Heads or Tails. If you are the 'matcher', you win when choices are identical. If you are the 'mismatche', you win when choices differ. Payoffs are equal and opposite — this is a zero-sum game. Your goal is to be unpredictable while predicting your opponent.
keyInsight: In zero-sum games with no pure-strategy equilibrium, the only rational play is to randomise equiprobably. Any detectable pattern — even a preference for Heads, or alternating too often — can be exploited by an observant opponent. True randomisation is the only unexploitable strategy.
lessons: There is no 'correct' pure strategy. Whatever you play, your opponent can exploit it. The Nash equilibrium is a mixed strategy: play each option with equal probability. In this equilibrium, your opponent gains nothing from knowing your strategy.

Humans are bad at generating random sequences. We tend to alternate too much (after H, we play T) and avoid long runs (three H in a row feels 'too lucky' to be random). This predictability can be exploited.
The minimax theorem: in zero-sum games, the optimal strategy minimises the maximum payoff your opponent can guarantee. This minimax and maximin coincide at the mixed strategy Nash equilibrium.
Mixed strategies are not the same as confused or random strategies. Mixing 50/50 in matching pennies is precisely optimal — not a sign of indecision. The randomness is strategic.

strategies.name: Always Heads
strategies.outcome: Immediately exploitable. Once your opponent notices you always play H, they can guarantee themselves a win every round by responding appropriately.
strategies.insight: Pure strategies in matching pennies are dominated by any mixture — even a 51/49 mix beats a pure strategy against an opponent who can detect it.

strategies.name: True 50/50 random mix
strategies.outcome: The Nash equilibrium. Your opponent cannot do better than 50% against you, regardless of their strategy. You cannot do better than 50% yourself. Both players earn zero in expectation.
strategies.insight: The equilibrium gives each player a guaranteed minimum expected payoff. Deviating from 50/50 never helps and can only hurt if the opponent exploits the deviation.

strategies.name: Exploit opponent's pattern
strategies.outcome: If your opponent alternates too much, play the opposite of their last choice. If they avoid long runs, play the same as their last choice after seeing two identical choices. Pattern exploitation earns above 50%.
strategies.insight: This is how professional poker and competitive sports players gain edges. If your opponent is not truly random, you can profit from their predictability.

classroomObservations: After the game, show the sequence of each player's choices and test for randomness (e.g., run test, autocorrelation). Students are almost always non-random — they alternate too regularly or avoid long runs. Ask: how would you generate a truly random sequence? The practical answer is a coin or a random number generator — human intuition fails.
realWorld: Penalty kicks in football (keeper and kicker play a matching pennies game), military deception operations, competitive poker (bluffing must be unpredictable), and randomised drug testing (if testing is predictable, athletes use substances on non-test days) all require mixed strategies.
tip: To win consistently, you need to either be more random than your opponent or detect and exploit their non-randomness. A coin flip is theoretically optimal. But watching for patterns and exploiting them is how real competitive advantages are built.
furtherReading: Von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944) — Theory of Games and Economic Behavior; Walker & Wooders (2001) — Minimax Play at Wimbledon; Chiappori, Levitt & Groseclose (2002) — Testing Mixed-Strategy Equilibria When Players Are Heterogeneous: The Case of Penalty Kicks in Soccer
numericalExample: Payoff: win = +1, lose = -1. If you always play Heads, opponent learns and always plays their winning response — you earn -1 every round. If you play 50/50 randomly, opponent earns 0 in expectation regardless of their strategy. If opponent alternates H,T,H,T... and you notice, play T,H,T,H... and earn +1 every round. Pattern detection is the key skill.

title: Cournot Competition
subtitle: Quantity Competition in Oligopoly
concept: Firms simultaneously choose quantities to produce. Each firm's profit depends on the market price, which is determined by total industry output. More output drives the price down for everyone. The Cournot Nash equilibrium sits between the monopoly outcome (restricted output, high price) and the competitive outcome (high output, low price).
setup: You are a firm competing with rivals in a market. You simultaneously choose how much to produce. The market price is determined by the total output of all firms — more total output means a lower price. Your profit is (price − cost) × your quantity. You don't see rivals' choices before committing.
keyInsight: More competitors → lower prices and higher total output. With two firms, profits are significantly above zero but below monopoly levels. As the number of firms grows, the Cournot equilibrium converges toward the competitive (zero-profit) outcome. Market concentration is directly linked to market power.
lessons: The best-response function: given what you think rivals will produce, your optimal quantity is one that equates your marginal revenue to marginal cost. The Cournot equilibrium is where all firms are on their best-response curves simultaneously.

The Cournot equilibrium produces more output than monopoly (better for consumers) but less than perfect competition (still some deadweight loss). It is a middle ground — market power persists with a small number of firms.

Collusion is profitable: if both firms restrict output to the joint-monopoly level, both earn more than the Cournot equilibrium. But each firm has a private incentive to produce more than its agreed quota — this is why cartels are unstable.
Market concentration and social welfare: the fewer firms there are, the higher prices are, the greater the deadweight loss, and the more antitrust enforcement matters.

strategies.name: Play the Cournot best-response quantity
strategies.outcome: The Nash equilibrium — no firm can increase profit by unilaterally changing quantity. Stable but inefficient (deadweight loss relative to competitive outcome).
strategies.insight: The best-response rule: produce half of (max market quantity − rivals' quantity). This means rivals' output crowds out your optimal production — reacting to rivals is the key skill.

strategies.name: Collude (produce monopoly quantity / n)
strategies.outcome: Everyone earns more than the Cournot equilibrium — total industry profit is maximised. But each individual firm profits by producing slightly more. Without enforcement, collusion unravels.
strategies.insight: Collusion is the prisoner's dilemma of markets. It is individually unstable even though it is collectively optimal. This is why antitrust law exists — and why cartels so often collapse.

strategies.name: Overproduce (quantity war)
strategies.outcome: Drives the market price down toward marginal cost. Industry profits collapse. Rivals either match or are forced to exit. Long-run outcome is closer to competitive equilibrium.
strategies.insight: Quantity wars are the Cournot equivalent of price wars. Aggressive expansion hurts everyone, including the aggressor. The outcome approaches Bertrand (price = cost) as firms keep expanding.

classroomObservations: Compare the actual average quantities chosen to the theoretical Cournot equilibrium and to the collusive optimum. Ask: why don't firms collude? What would it take to sustain collusion? (Communication, monitoring, enforcement.) This connects directly to OPEC, airline alliances, and cartel prosecutions.
realWorld: OPEC member quotas, duopoly airline routes, pharmaceutical markets after generic entry, telecommunications infrastructure sharing, and supermarket price coordination all exhibit Cournot-like dynamics. The number of competitors is the key variable — it determines how far from monopoly pricing the market sits.
tip: The Cournot best-response formula is: q* = (a − c − Q_rivals) / 2, where a is market demand intercept, c is marginal cost, and Q_rivals is total rival production. If you think rivals will produce more, you produce less — and vice versa.
furtherReading: Cournot (1838) — Researches into the Mathematical Principles of the Theory of Wealth; Tirole (1988) — The Theory of Industrial Organization (Ch. 5); Bresnahan (1989) — Empirical Studies of Industries with Market Power
numericalExample: Market demand: P = 100 - Q_total. Marginal cost = 10. Monopoly: Q=45, P=$55, profit=$2,025. Cournot duopoly: each firm produces 30, total Q=60, P=$40, each profit=$900 (total $1,800). Perfect competition: Q=90, P=$10, profit=$0. Adding one competitor cuts price by $15 and total profit by $225.

title: Bertrand Competition
subtitle: Price Competition & the Bertrand Paradox
concept: Firms simultaneously set prices for identical products. Any firm that prices above marginal cost loses all customers to the cheapest rival (since goods are identical and customers buy from the lowest-price seller). The Bertrand Nash equilibrium is price = marginal cost — even with only two firms. This is the Bertrand Paradox.
setup: You are a firm selling an identical product to rivals. Customers always buy from the cheapest seller. You and rivals simultaneously set prices. If you match the lowest price, you share the market equally. If you undercut, you capture the whole market. If you price higher, you sell nothing. Your profit is (price − cost) × your sales volume.
keyInsight: Two firms are sufficient for competitive pricing. In Cournot competition, two firms earn significant profits. In Bertrand competition with identical goods, two firms earn zero. The reason: any price above cost invites undercutting. The equilibrium is price = marginal cost, regardless of how few firms there are.
lessons: The Bertrand Paradox: the market structure (duopoly vs. competitive market) doesn't matter for pricing when goods are identical. Two firms are enough to eliminate market power. This is economically surprising — concentration usually predicts pricing power.

The paradox is resolved in practice by: product differentiation (goods aren't actually identical), capacity constraints (can't serve all customers even at the right price), switching costs, and repeated interaction (tacit collusion).

Price competition is much fiercer than quantity competition. Bertrand markets look like competitive markets; Cournot markets look like oligopolies. The mode of competition (price vs. quantity) matters enormously.
Undercutting is the dominant strategy in the short run but triggers retaliation. The only stable point is p = MC, where no further undercutting is profitable.

strategies.name: Price at marginal cost
strategies.outcome: The Nash equilibrium. Zero economic profit but no incentive for rivals to undercut further. The market clears efficiently — all consumers who value the good above cost buy it.
strategies.insight: The most competitive outcome possible. If every firm prices here, the market is identical to perfect competition — even with just two firms.

strategies.name: Price above marginal cost
strategies.outcome: You earn positive margin per unit but lose all customers to any rival who undercuts by even one cent. Only sustainable if rivals also price high — which requires collusion or differentiation.
strategies.insight: This is the core Bertrand result: any price above cost is unstable. Competition always drives prices to cost in homogeneous-goods markets.

strategies.name: Undercut rivals repeatedly
strategies.outcome: Triggers a price war that ends at p = MC. You capture the whole market briefly, but rivals match you immediately. Total industry profit collapses to zero.
strategies.insight: Price wars are mutually destructive. Both firms end up at zero profit. The lesson for real businesses: avoid Bertrand competition by differentiating your product.

classroomObservations: Show how quickly prices converge to marginal cost — even in a duopoly. This shocks students who expect two firms to have market power. Ask: what would have to change for these firms to earn profits? This leads naturally to the real-world strategies firms use to escape Bertrand: branding, patents, loyalty programmes, switching costs.
realWorld: Commodity markets (wheat, oil), e-commerce price comparison (Amazon vs. rivals for identical products), generic pharmaceutical entry, and airline route pricing with identical service all exhibit Bertrand pressure. Companies invest heavily in branding and differentiation precisely to escape the zero-profit Bertrand outcome.
tip: Bertrand competition only leads to zero profits with truly homogeneous goods and unlimited capacity. Add differentiation (different brands, locations, quality), capacity limits, or search costs — and market power returns immediately.
furtherReading: Bertrand (1883) — Book review of Cournot's work; Edgeworth (1897) — La Teoria Pura del Monopolio; Tirole (1988) — The Theory of Industrial Organization (Ch. 5-6)
numericalExample: Two firms, MC=$10. If Firm A prices $20 and Firm B prices $19, all customers go to B. Firm B earns ($19-$10) x total demand. A earns $0. A then prices $18 — all customers switch back. This continues until both price at $10 = MC, earning $0 profit. Two firms are enough to replicate perfect competition — the Bertrand paradox.

title: Monopoly Pricing
subtitle: Market Power, Deadweight Loss & Consumer Welfare
concept: A monopolist faces no competition and so can set price above marginal cost. It maximises profit by choosing output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost — which implies a price higher than the competitive level. The welfare cost of this is deadweight loss: profitable trades that don't happen because the price is too high.
setup: You are the only seller in a market. You choose a price (or quantity), and demand determines how many units you sell. Higher prices mean fewer sales. Your goal is to maximise profit: revenue minus cost. The efficient outcome (price = marginal cost) gives you zero profit. The monopoly optimum gives you maximum profit at the cost of some consumers being priced out of the market.
keyInsight: Monopoly pricing is privately rational but socially inefficient. The gap between price and marginal cost is the Lerner Index — a measure of market power. The deadweight loss triangle represents the value of trades that would benefit both buyer and seller but do not occur because the monopolist restricts output.
lessons: The profit-maximising rule is MR = MC. For a linear demand curve, the monopoly quantity is exactly half the competitive quantity — so the monopolist produces half as much as a competitive market and charges the maximum price that would clear that quantity.

Deadweight loss is the social cost of monopoly power. It represents consumer and producer surplus that is destroyed — value that nobody gets. It grows with the elasticity of demand and the size of the price-cost margin.

Price discrimination can eliminate deadweight loss: if the monopolist charges each consumer their exact willingness to pay, output is maximised and no surplus is destroyed. But this requires the monopolist to extract all consumer surplus.
Regulation responses: price-cap regulation (set p = MC or p = AC), public ownership, or breaking up the monopoly. Each has trade-offs between efficiency, access, and investment incentives.

strategies.name: Price at the monopoly optimum (MR = MC)
strategies.outcome: Maximises your profit. A fraction of potential customers are priced out of the market. Deadweight loss is created — value that could exist doesn't.
strategies.insight: The privately optimal choice is socially inefficient. This is the core market failure that motivates antitrust and regulation.

strategies.name: Price too high
strategies.outcome: Fewer units sold than optimal. Revenue and profit both fall. You have less market power than you think — high prices reduce both volume and total profit.
strategies.insight: There is such a thing as pricing too high for a monopolist: the revenue loss from fewer sales outweighs the margin gain. The MR = MC rule is the sweet spot.

strategies.name: Price at marginal cost
strategies.outcome: Zero economic profit for you — but socially efficient. Maximum consumer surplus. This is what regulation tries to achieve but struggles to sustain because the firm needs to cover fixed costs.
strategies.insight: P = MC is the social optimum but gives the firm no profit. This is why natural monopolies (like utilities) are regulated at average cost (P = AC), which allows cost recovery while limiting market power.

classroomObservations: Show the demand curve, the MR curve, and the MC line. Draw the deadweight loss triangle. Ask students: how large would the deadweight loss have to be before regulation is worthwhile? This brings in the cost of regulation vs. the cost of monopoly. Compare monopoly output to competitive output — the factor-of-2 relationship is a clean, memorable result.
realWorld: Pharmaceutical patents create temporary monopolies to incentivise R&D — the trade-off between static efficiency (low prices now) and dynamic efficiency (innovation). Platform monopolies (Google Search, OS markets), utility companies, and copyright holders all exercise monopoly pricing power with varying welfare consequences.
tip: Lerner Index = (P − MC) / P = 1 / |price elasticity of demand|. A monopolist with perfectly inelastic demand (elasticity = 0) charges an infinite markup — this never happens in practice because there are always substitutes.
furtherReading: Lerner (1934) — The Concept of Monopoly and the Measurement of Monopoly Power; Baumol & Bradford (1970) — Optimal Departures from Marginal Cost Pricing; Shapiro & Varian (1999) — Information Rules
numericalExample: Demand: P=100-Q, MC=10. Monopoly: MR=100-2Q=10, so Q*=45, P*=$55. Profit = (55-10)x45 = $2,025. Competitive: P=MC=$10, Q=90. Deadweight loss = 0.5 x (55-10) x (90-45) = $1,012.50. The monopolist destroys $1,012 of value that could exist — value that benefits no one.

title: English Auction
subtitle: Ascending Bid Auctions & Revenue Equivalence
concept: In an English auction, bidders raise bids openly until only one remains willing to bid. The winner pays just above the second-highest bidder's value. With independent private values (each bidder knows their own value, not others'), the dominant strategy is to continue bidding up to your true value — no more, no less.
setup: An item is auctioned. You know your own private value for it (how much it is worth to you). Bids increase in open increments. When the price exceeds your value, you drop out. The last remaining bidder wins and pays the current bid price. Your profit is your value minus what you pay — or zero if you don't win.
keyInsight: Truthful bidding (bidding up to your value) is a dominant strategy. You win every auction where you are the highest-value bidder, and you never overpay because you only beat the second-highest value by the minimum increment. This makes the English auction efficient: the highest-value bidder always wins.
lessons: Bidding above your value is always irrational: even if you win, you pay more than the item is worth to you — a loss. Bidding below your value is also costly: you may lose auctions where winning would have been profitable.

Revenue equivalence theorem: under standard conditions, the expected revenue to the seller is the same in English auctions, sealed-bid second-price auctions, first-price auctions, and Dutch auctions. The format changes strategy but not expected revenue.

The winner's curse applies to common-value auctions (where all bidders would assign the same value to the item if they had full information — e.g. oil field rights, company acquisitions). In this game with private values, there is no winner's curse — but students should understand when to apply caution.
Ascending price formats tend to be more efficient in private-value settings because dropping out reveals information that helps remaining bidders calibrate their strategies.

strategies.name: Bid up to your true value
strategies.outcome: The dominant strategy. You win when it is profitable and don't win when it is not. Your surplus is (your value − final price). You cannot improve on this by bidding differently.
strategies.insight: Dominant strategy: it is best regardless of what others do. This makes English auctions easy to play optimally — just be honest about your maximum willingness to pay.

strategies.name: Stop early (bid below your value)
strategies.outcome: You may lose auctions you could have won profitably. You see others are still bidding — the current price is below your value. Leaving money on the table by dropping out early.
strategies.insight: Shading your bid costs you profitable wins. Unlike in sealed-bid first-price auctions, there is no reason to shade in an ascending auction because you only pay just above the second-highest bid.

strategies.name: Bid above your value
strategies.outcome: You might win, but if you pay more than your value, you make a loss on the transaction. The 'winner's curse' — but in a private-value setting you have no excuse for this error.
strategies.insight: Overbidding happens when bidders get caught up in the excitement of bidding wars. Set a firm maximum before bidding starts.

classroomObservations: Check whether the highest-value bidder won. They should in a well-designed English auction with rational bidders. Show the distribution of private values and the final price. Ask: what is the seller's revenue? Is it close to the second-highest value? The gap is the auctioneer's format choice between revenue maximisation and efficiency.
realWorld: Sotheby's and Christie's art auctions, eBay (timed ascending bid format), Google's initial public offering (Dutch auction variant), FCC spectrum auctions, and estate sales all use variants of the English auction. Treasury bonds use a uniform-price sealed-bid auction — similar in structure.
tip: Before the auction, write down the maximum you are willing to pay and do not exceed it. In the heat of bidding, psychological pressure pushes bids above rational limits — the 'bidding frenzy' is a real bias that costs real money.
furtherReading: Vickrey (1961) — Counterspeculation, Auctions, and Competitive Sealed Tenders (Nobel Prize 1996); Klemperer (2004) — Auctions: Theory and Practice; Milgrom & Weber (1982) — A Theory of Auctions and Competitive Bidding
numericalExample: 3 bidders with private values $80, $60, $40. Dominant strategy: bid your true value. Bidder 1 wins, pays $60 (second-highest value) + minimum increment. Bidder 1's surplus = $80-$60 = $20. Bidder 2 earns $0. If Bidder 1 had bid $100 (overbid), they still win and still pay $60 — no benefit. If they bid $50 (underbid), they lose to Bidder 2 and miss $20 of surplus.

title: Ad Auction
subtitle: Sponsored Search & Generalised Second-Price Auctions
concept: Advertisers bid for ranked positions in search results. Each position receives a different number of clicks. Advertisers pay per click, and the price they pay is determined by the bid of the advertiser ranked just below them — a generalised second-price (GSP) auction. Higher bids win higher positions but may not always be worth the premium.
setup: You are an advertiser bidding for a slot on a search results page. Higher-ranked slots get more clicks. You know how much each click is worth to you (your per-click value). You submit a bid. Slots are assigned highest-bid-first. You pay the bid of the advertiser just below you per click received.
keyInsight: The GSP auction is not perfectly incentive-compatible — unlike the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism, truthful bidding is not always optimal for every position. But it approximately encourages honest bidding, and its simplicity is why it dominates real-world advertising markets.
lessons: The top slot gets the most clicks but costs the most per click (you pay just above the second bidder). It is only worth the premium if your per-click value is high enough that the extra clicks more than offset the higher price.

The key question is: is the marginal click from a higher position worth the marginal cost? This depends on click-through rate differences between positions, your conversion rate, and your profit per conversion.

Unlike a standard Vickrey auction, optimal bidding in GSP can involve strategic shading — bidding slightly below your true value to win a lower position at a lower price per click. But the gains from sophisticated play are usually small.

Quality scores matter: in Google's real auction, your bid is multiplied by your Quality Score (historical click-through rate, relevance score). A highly relevant ad can outrank a higher bid by being more likely to be clicked.

strategies.name: Bid your true per-click value
strategies.outcome: Simple and approximately optimal. You win the highest position where your value exceeds your cost per click. Prevents you from winning positions at a loss.
strategies.insight: Truthful bidding is a reasonable heuristic even though it is not perfectly optimal in GSP. The gains from sophisticated strategic play rarely justify the complexity.

strategies.name: Overbid for top position
strategies.outcome: Wins the top slot but pays more per click than it generates in revenue. Profitable only if your conversion rate or revenue per conversion is high enough to justify the premium.
strategies.insight: Brand advertisers often pay for top position even when the cost-per-click economics are marginal — because visibility itself has value. Performance advertisers should only pay for clicks that convert.

strategies.name: Underbid for a lower-cost position
strategies.outcome: Pays a lower price per click. Only rational if click quality is similar across positions or if the volume reduction is offset by cost savings.
strategies.insight: Lower positions can be better value for advertisers with high conversion rates, since the traffic they receive is smaller but cheaper. Position 2 or 3 can outperform position 1 on a cost-per-acquisition basis.

classroomObservations: Show the slot assignment, click volumes, prices paid, and profit earned for each bidder. Ask: who won the most money — the highest bidder or the most efficient bidder? This reveals that winning the top slot is not always the optimal strategy. Discuss how Google's Quality Score system changes incentives — it aligns advertiser relevance with user experience.
realWorld: Google Ads, Meta Ads, Amazon sponsored listings, and LinkedIn ads all use GSP-style auctions. Digital advertising is a $600 billion industry that runs almost entirely on these mechanisms. The economic insight — that well-designed auctions align private incentives with efficient allocation — is one of the most impactful applications of auction theory.
tip: Calculate your expected profit per position before bidding: (your per-click value − price per click) × clicks received. Bid up to the value where expected profit goes to zero. Don't pay for clicks that cost more than they earn.
furtherReading: Edelman, Ostrovsky & Schwarz (2007) — Internet Advertising and the Generalised Second-Price Auction; Varian (2007) — Position Auctions; Myerson (1981) — Optimal Auction Design (Nobel Prize 2007)
numericalExample: 3 ad slots: Slot 1=1,000 clicks/day, Slot 2=600 clicks/day, Slot 3=300 clicks/day. Your value-per-click=$0.50. Slot 1 costs $0.40/click (bid of #2 advertiser): profit = (0.50-0.40)x1,000 = $100/day. Slot 2 costs $0.30/click: profit = (0.50-0.30)x600 = $120/day. Slot 2 is more profitable than Slot 1 despite fewer clicks — the cost savings outweigh the volume loss.

title: Double Auction
subtitle: Market Price Discovery & Competitive Equilibrium
concept: Both buyers and sellers submit offers simultaneously. A buyer's bid states the maximum they'll pay; a seller's ask states the minimum they'll accept. Trades occur when a bid meets or exceeds an ask. The double auction is remarkably efficient at discovering the competitive equilibrium price — even with very few traders and without any central coordination.
setup: Buyers know their private value for the good (maximum willingness to pay); sellers know their private cost (minimum acceptable price). All buyers and sellers simultaneously submit bids and asks. Trades are executed whenever bid ≥ ask. Your profit as a buyer is (your value − price paid); as a seller, it is (price received − your cost).
keyInsight: Markets aggregate dispersed private information through prices — without any individual knowing the full picture. This is Hayek's insight. Even with self-interested traders who know only their own values and costs, the double auction consistently converges to the competitive equilibrium price within a few trading rounds.
lessons: Smith's (1962) experiments shocked economists: with just a handful of traders, double auctions converged reliably to the competitive equilibrium price. Markets 'work' even without many traders, perfect information, or a central auctioneer.

The competitive equilibrium is efficient: all trades that are mutually beneficial occur. Buyers with values above the equilibrium price buy; sellers with costs below the equilibrium price sell. No profitable trade is missed.

Strategic shading is rational but limited in impact. Buyers want to bid below their value to buy cheap; sellers want to ask above their cost to sell high. But bid too low (or ask too high) and you don't trade at all.

Price discovery is the process by which the equilibrium price emerges from decentralised trading. It works best with many traders, low search costs, and standardised goods — the conditions of financial markets.

strategies.name: Buyers: bid close to your value
strategies.outcome: You trade when it is profitable and don't trade when it isn't. Bidding too low means missing out on profitable trades. The cost of shading is failing to execute.
strategies.insight: In thin markets (few traders), shading is more valuable — you have more pricing power. In deep markets, competition forces bids close to values.

strategies.name: Sellers: ask close to your cost
strategies.outcome: You trade when it is profitable. Asking too high means no trade; asking too low leaves surplus on the table. The market price (determined by competitive bids) sets your upper bound.
strategies.insight: Sellers with costs well below equilibrium price can ask well above cost and still trade. Sellers near the margin have little pricing power.

strategies.name: Strategic manipulation (thin market)
strategies.outcome: With few traders, submitting extreme bids or asks can move the market price in your favour. This is market power — it is more profitable but reduces overall market efficiency.
strategies.insight: Market power and market efficiency are inversely related. This is why competition authorities are more concerned about thin markets with few participants.

classroomObservations: Plot bid prices and ask prices on a supply/demand diagram. Show the competitive equilibrium. Show where actual trades occurred relative to the equilibrium price. In a well-functioning double auction, trades cluster around the equilibrium. Ask: what prevented some trades from occurring? Discuss the role of information asymmetry, search costs, and market thickness.
realWorld: Stock exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ, LSE), commodity futures markets (Chicago Mercantile Exchange), foreign exchange markets, and electricity markets all use continuous double-auction mechanisms. High-frequency trading firms earn profits by exploiting tiny inefficiencies in the price discovery process.
tip: Your optimal strategy depends on your private value or cost relative to the expected equilibrium price. If your value is well above equilibrium, bid aggressively — you can pay close to your value and still profit. If your value is near the margin, bid carefully — you have little room for error.
furtherReading: Smith (1962) — An Experimental Study of Competitive Market Behavior (Nobel Prize 2002); Hayek (1945) — The Use of Knowledge in Society; Gode & Sunder (1993) — Allocative Efficiency of Markets with Zero-Intelligence Traders
numericalExample: 5 buyers (values $90,$80,$70,$60,$50), 5 sellers (costs $30,$40,$50,$60,$70). Equilibrium P=$60, 4 trades. Total surplus = $30+$20+$10+$0 = $60. Smith found this equilibrium is reached within 2-3 rounds in the lab — even with no information sharing between traders. The price mechanism aggregates dispersed private information automatically.

title: Fishery
subtitle: Tragedy of the Commons & Common-Pool Resources
concept: A shared fishery is a common-pool resource: rival (one person's harvest reduces stock for others) but non-excludable (hard to prevent anyone from fishing). Each fisher ignores the cost their harvest imposes on others — they capture all the private benefit but share the cost. The individually rational choice (harvest as much as possible) destroys the collective resource.
setup: Players share a fishery with a regenerating fish stock. Each round you choose how many fish to harvest. The stock regenerates between rounds — but only if enough fish remain. If the total harvest exceeds the regeneration capacity, the stock declines. If the stock collapses, there are no fish left for anyone. Your goal is to maximise your cumulative harvest over the game.
keyInsight: Open-access common-pool resources are systematically over-exploited in the Nash equilibrium. Each individual acts rationally, but the collective result is resource depletion. This is Hardin's Tragedy of the Commons — not a failure of morality, but a failure of incentive structure.
lessons: In open access (no property rights, no regulation), the Nash equilibrium is over-exploitation. Each fisher's optimal response is to harvest more — until the stock collapses. This is the equilibrium even though it is collectively disastrous.

The sustainable harvest level (maximum sustainable yield) is the amount that can be taken every period without depleting the stock. It requires all players to cooperate — restraining their individual harvest below the privately optimal level.

Ostrom's insight: private property rights and government regulation are not the only solutions. Well-designed community governance — with clear rules, monitoring, and graduated sanctions — can sustain cooperation even in common-pool resources.

The three standard solutions: privatisation (assign property rights so the owner internalises the full cost of depletion), regulation (quota systems, licences, taxes), and Ostrom-style community governance (local rules, peer enforcement).

strategies.name: Harvest conservatively (sustainable level)
strategies.outcome: Preserves the fishery and earns a steady long-term income. But you are exploited if others over-harvest — the stock still depletes, and your restraint benefits free-riders.
strategies.insight: Conservation only works collectively. Unilateral restraint is altruistic but not sufficient — and not individually rational if others are over-harvesting.

strategies.name: Maximise personal harvest each round
strategies.outcome: Short-run gains but collapses the fishery within a few rounds. Once the stock is depleted, everyone earns zero — including you. The Nash equilibrium in open access.
strategies.insight: The tragedy is that this is privately rational right up to the moment of collapse. Each additional fish you take is worth more to you than its cost to you — even though the cost to the group is high.

strategies.name: Cooperate and agree on quotas
strategies.outcome: The efficient outcome — maximises long-run total harvest. Requires communication, monitoring (can you trust others to respect their quota?), and enforcement (what happens to cheaters?).
strategies.insight: Voluntary cooperation works when groups are small, members know each other, violations are observable, and sanctions are credible. These are exactly Ostrom's conditions for successful self-governance.

classroomObservations: Show the stock level across rounds — the depletion trajectory is stark. Ask students: when did you first realise the fishery was in trouble? Why didn't you cut back then? This reveals the collective action problem in real time. Then ask: what rule change would have produced a better outcome? This connects the game to real fishery management policy.
realWorld: Atlantic cod collapse (Canada, 1990s), groundwater depletion (Ogallala Aquifer, US), deforestation, ocean plastic pollution, and congestion on public roads all follow the tragedy of the commons structure. Tradeable permits (carbon markets), fishing quotas, and Ostrom's community governance models are real policy responses.
tip: Watch the stock level indicator carefully. Once it starts falling, it accelerates — depletion is non-linear. The time to act is before the stock drops below the regeneration threshold, not after.
furtherReading: Hardin (1968) — The Tragedy of the Commons; Ostrom (1990) — Governing the Commons (Nobel Prize 2009); Gordon (1954) — The Economic Theory of a Common-Property Resource: The Fishery
numericalExample: Stock=100 fish, regeneration=20%/round, 5 players. Sustainable harvest per player = 20 total / 5 = 4 fish/round. If everyone takes 4: stock stays at 100, each earns 4/round forever. If each takes 10: total harvest=50, stock falls to 50, regeneration=10, next round stock=60... then 52... then 42... collapse in ~7 rounds. Nash equilibrium = over-harvest = eventual zero earnings.
