title: Bank Run
subtitle: Coordination Failure & Self-Fulfilling Crises
concept: Banks borrow short (deposits) and lend long (illiquid loans). If all depositors withdraw simultaneously, the bank must liquidate assets at a loss and may fail — even if it would have been solvent otherwise. The run is self-fulfilling: if you believe others will run, it is rational to run too, which causes the very crisis you feared.
setup: You are a depositor in a bank. The bank has invested your deposits in long-term assets. If you withdraw early, you get your full deposit back (the bank liquidates assets at a discount to pay you). If the bank stays open and you wait, you earn the full return. But if too many depositors withdraw, the bank fails and late withdrawers get nothing.
keyInsight: Bank runs are a coordination failure with two equilibria: 'no run' (everyone waits, the bank stays solvent, everyone earns the full return) and 'run' (everyone withdraws, the bank fails, early movers recover their deposits, late movers get nothing). Both are self-fulfilling. Which equilibrium occurs depends on beliefs.
lessons: The bank run is a prisoner's dilemma: if you believe others won't run, you should wait (better returns). If you believe others will run, you should run first (recover your deposit before the bank fails). Expectations drive the outcome.

Deposit insurance eliminates the run equilibrium by guaranteeing deposits regardless of what others do. Once 'wait' is always safe, 'run' is never rational — the coordination failure disappears. This is why deposit insurance was introduced after the Great Depression bank panics.

Solvent banks can fail due to runs — the crisis is not caused by underlying insolvency but by coordinated panic. This is the key insight of Diamond & Dybvig: banking fragility is intrinsic to the maturity mismatch, not just to bad loans.
Central banks act as lenders of last resort for the same reason: by guaranteeing to lend to solvent banks under pressure, they eliminate the run equilibrium before it starts.

strategies.name: Wait (don't run)
strategies.outcome: Best outcome if others also wait — you earn the full return on your deposits. Catastrophic if others run and you wait too long — you are last in the queue when the bank has already failed.
strategies.insight: Waiting is optimal in the 'good' equilibrium. The risk is being caught in the 'bad' equilibrium — where others have already decided to run.

strategies.name: Run (withdraw immediately)
strategies.outcome: Safe regardless of what others do — you get your deposit back before the bank potentially fails. But if everyone runs, this precipitates the bank failure that motivates the run in the first place.
strategies.insight: Running is individually rational under panic but collectively self-defeating. Each runner is rational; the aggregate is disastrous.

strategies.name: Wait if you receive credible information the bank is solvent
strategies.outcome: The socially optimal strategy requires credible, public information about bank health. Transparency, stress tests, and central bank backstops are designed to provide this credibility.
strategies.insight: Sunspot equilibria: runs can be triggered by irrelevant public signals (a rumour, a news headline) that coordinate depositor expectations. Regulation aims to eliminate these multiple equilibria.

classroomObservations: Show the two equilibrium outcomes side by side: what each depositor earns if everyone waits vs. what they earn if everyone runs. The 'run' equilibrium is individually rational but collectively disastrous. Ask: what information would make you confident enough to wait? This reveals the role of transparency and credibility in financial stability.
realWorld: Northern Rock (UK, 2007) — queues around the block from a Twitter rumour. Silicon Valley Bank (US, 2023) — fastest bank run in history, driven by instant digital withdrawals. The Great Depression — 9,000 bank failures in the 1930s before deposit insurance. Each case illustrates how coordination failure can destroy solvent institutions.
tip: Ask yourself: do I believe the bank is solvent? Do I believe others believe the bank is solvent? It is not enough to know the bank is safe — you also need to believe others know it. This is the game of higher-order beliefs that drives crises.
furtherReading: Diamond & Dybvig (1983) — Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity (Nobel Prize 2022); Kindleberger (1978) — Manias, Panics, and Crashes; Calomiris & Gorton (1991) — The Origins of Banking Panics
numericalExample: Bank has $1,000 in deposits, invested in assets worth $1,200 if held to maturity but only $900 if liquidated early. 100 depositors, each with $10. If 90 run: bank liquidates $900, pays 90 runners $10 each, last 10 depositors get $0. If 0 run: all get $12 at maturity. The $2 gain from waiting vs. the $10 loss from being last drives the panic.

title: Asset Bubble
subtitle: Speculation, Momentum & the Greater Fool Theory
concept: Asset prices can rise far above fundamental value when traders believe they can sell to a 'greater fool' at a higher price. Each trader may know the asset is overvalued but buys anyway — expecting to exit before the crash. Bubbles are rational at the individual level yet collectively destabilising.
setup: Players buy and sell an asset across multiple rounds. The asset has a known fundamental value (the present value of its cash flows). The market price is determined by supply and demand. Players can buy if they think the price will rise further, or sell if they think the peak has passed. The bubble eventually collapses to fundamental value — but the timing is uncertain.
keyInsight: Bubbles can be rational even when everyone knows the asset is overpriced. The greater fool theory: as long as there is a buyer willing to pay more, buying at an inflated price can be profitable. Bubbles collapse when the pool of greater fools runs out — and no one can predict exactly when that is.
lessons: The fundamental value of an asset is the present value of all future cash flows. When price diverges from fundamental value, it is a bubble. But 'knowing' this doesn't help you profit from it — you still need to time your exit correctly.
Keynes's observation: 'Markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent.' Short-selling a bubble is dangerous because the bubble can inflate far further before collapsing.

Feedback loops sustain bubbles: rising prices attract more buyers (momentum trading), which raises prices further, which attracts more buyers. This is positive feedback — the opposite of the negative feedback that keeps equilibrium prices stable.

Crashes are typically sudden and severe. The bubble collapses when expectations shift — either from a triggering event or from a critical mass of sellers. The shift from inflated to fundamental value can happen in days.

strategies.name: Buy early, sell before peak
strategies.outcome: Highly profitable if you time it correctly. Requires either superior information about when the bubble will burst or a disciplined exit rule (e.g. 'sell when price exceeds 2× fundamental value').
strategies.insight: Bubbles make early entrants rich and late entrants poor. The difference between a smart speculator and a greater fool is timing — and timing is notoriously unreliable.

strategies.name: Buy and hold through the crash
strategies.outcome: You eventually receive the fundamental value — but you gave up the opportunity to sell high. If you paid inflated prices, you incur a loss. Long-run investors avoid this by not buying above fundamental value.
strategies.insight: Buy-and-hold strategies protect against bubble losses only if you buy at or below fundamental value. Buying into a bubble and holding is not the same as long-term investing.

strategies.name: Never buy above fundamental value
strategies.outcome: You miss speculative gains but avoid catastrophic losses. You purchase only when price ≤ fundamental value and sell when it rises above. Boring but reliable.
strategies.insight: Value investing: buy what is cheap relative to fundamentals. This is Buffett's approach. It requires patience and the ability to sit out bubbles while watching others profit — psychologically very difficult.

classroomObservations: Show the price path vs. the fundamental value line. The gap is the bubble. Ask: at what point did you know it was a bubble? Why did you keep buying (or holding)? This reveals the psychological forces that sustain bubbles — FOMO, herding, overconfidence, and the conviction that 'this time is different'.
realWorld: Tulip mania (1637), South Sea Bubble (1720), dot-com bubble (1999-2001), US housing bubble (2003-2008), and cryptocurrency cycles all share the same structure: prices rise far above fundamentals, sustained by expectations of further gains, and crash suddenly when those expectations reverse.
tip: The question is not 'is this a bubble?' but 'when will it pop?' Bubbles can last far longer than fundamental analysis suggests. If you trade in a bubble, set a hard exit price before you enter — decision-making under euphoria is unreliable.
furtherReading: Shiller (2000) — Irrational Exuberance; Kindleberger (1978) — Manias, Panics, and Crashes; Brunnermeier (2008) — Bubbles, entry in New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics
numericalExample: Asset fundamental value = $10. In round 1 price rises to $15 (50% above fundamental). A trader buys at $15 expecting to sell at $20. If everyone does this and price reaches $20, early buyers profit $5. But when the last buyer has no one to sell to, the crash is sudden: price falls to $10 in one round. The last buyer loses $10. Winner = early movers. Loser = whoever holds when music stops.

title: Portfolio Frontier
subtitle: Diversification, Mean-Variance Optimisation & the Efficient Frontier
concept: By combining assets whose returns are not perfectly correlated, investors can reduce portfolio risk without sacrificing expected return. The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios that offer the maximum expected return for each level of risk (standard deviation). Portfolios below the frontier are inefficient — dominated by something better.
setup: You choose portfolio weights across multiple assets, each with different expected returns and volatilities. The return and risk of your portfolio depend on both the individual assets and the correlations between them. Your goal is to build the portfolio with the highest expected return for a given level of risk you are willing to accept.
keyInsight: Diversification is the only free lunch in finance. Combining two risky assets almost always reduces total portfolio risk when their returns are not perfectly correlated — without reducing the weighted average expected return. The efficient frontier shows exactly how much risk reduction is achievable through optimal combinations.
lessons: Risk has two components: systematic risk (affecting all assets — macroeconomic shocks, interest rates) cannot be diversified away. Idiosyncratic risk (specific to one company — management failures, product recalls) can be eliminated by holding enough assets.

Correlation is the key variable. Two assets with returns that are negatively correlated (move in opposite directions) provide maximum diversification benefit — the portfolio variance can be lower than either individual asset's variance.

The minimum-variance portfolio has the lowest risk possible. The tangency portfolio has the highest Sharpe ratio (return per unit of risk). CAPM says every investor should hold the tangency portfolio combined with the risk-free asset — this is the market portfolio.

Mean-variance optimisation is sensitive to input estimates. Small errors in expected return estimates cause large changes in optimal weights. In practice, portfolios often use equal weights or factor models rather than exact optimisation to avoid overfitting.

strategies.name: Hold a single high-return asset
strategies.outcome: Bears all idiosyncratic risk of that asset. Never on the efficient frontier unless all assets are perfectly correlated. You are taking undiversified risk that earns no extra expected return.
strategies.insight: Concentrated portfolios are only rational if you have genuine informational edge on a specific asset. Without edge, concentration is just uncompensated risk.

strategies.name: Build a diversified portfolio on the efficient frontier
strategies.outcome: Achieves the best attainable risk-return combination. The specific point on the frontier depends on your risk tolerance — more risk-averse investors choose portfolios closer to the minimum-variance point.
strategies.insight: Efficient portfolios dominate inefficient ones: for the same expected return, you take less risk. There is no reason to hold an inefficient portfolio if a better one is available.

strategies.name: Hold the market index portfolio
strategies.outcome: According to CAPM, this is the tangency portfolio — the best risky portfolio for any investor. Combined with the risk-free asset, it generates any desired risk-return combination on the capital market line.
strategies.insight: Index investing is mean-variance optimal under CAPM assumptions. The practical implication: low-cost index funds are hard to beat on a risk-adjusted basis after fees.

classroomObservations: Show the efficient frontier diagram with individual assets plotted inside it. Ask: why are some portfolios outside the frontier? (They are not — individual assets are inside, never outside.) Point to the minimum-variance portfolio and the tangency portfolio. Ask: where on the frontier would a very risk-averse investor choose? A risk-neutral one?
realWorld: Pension funds (liability-driven investment), endowment funds (Yale model), risk-parity strategies (Bridgewater's All Weather fund), and robo-advisors (Betterment, Wealthfront) all implement mean-variance thinking. The shift from active stock-picking to passive index investing over the last 40 years is partly a practical application of portfolio theory.
tip: Correlation between assets is what drives diversification benefit. An asset with low expected return but negative correlation with your existing portfolio can still be valuable — it reduces risk without adding much. Don't evaluate assets in isolation; evaluate them as additions to an existing portfolio.
furtherReading: Markowitz (1952) — Portfolio Selection (Nobel Prize 1990); Sharpe (1964) — Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium Under Conditions of Risk; Fama & French (1992) — The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns
numericalExample: Asset A: return 10%, std dev 20%. Asset B: return 10%, std dev 20%. If correlation = +1.0: 50/50 portfolio std dev = 20% (no diversification benefit). If correlation = 0: portfolio std dev = 14.1% (same return, 30% less risk). If correlation = -1.0: portfolio std dev = 0% (zero risk, 10% return — the perfect hedge). Correlation is everything.

title: Monte Carlo Pi
subtitle: Simulation, Randomness & the Law of Large Numbers
concept: Random points are scattered uniformly inside a unit square. The fraction that fall inside the inscribed quarter-circle estimates π/4. As the number of points grows, the estimate converges to the true value. This illustrates Monte Carlo simulation: using random sampling to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute analytically.
setup: Random points are generated in a square. Each point is tested: does it fall inside the inscribed circle? The ratio of points inside the circle to total points estimates π/4. Your contribution is adding more sample points — each one refines the estimate. The law of large numbers guarantees convergence, but convergence is slow.
keyInsight: Randomness can solve deterministic problems. Monte Carlo methods approximate values that are hard to compute exactly by simulating the underlying random process and averaging the results. The accuracy improves with the square root of the number of samples — doubling precision requires quadrupling the sample size.
lessons: The Law of Large Numbers: the sample average converges to the population mean as the sample size grows. With enough samples, any Monte Carlo estimate becomes arbitrarily accurate — but 'enough' can be very large.

Error scales as 1/√n: to reduce estimation error by half, you need 4× as many samples. To gain one decimal place of accuracy, you need 100× more samples. This slow convergence is the fundamental cost of Monte Carlo methods.

Variance reduction techniques make Monte Carlo more efficient without adding samples: stratified sampling (divide the space into regions and sample from each), antithetic variates (use paired correlated samples), and importance sampling (oversample from the most important regions).

Monte Carlo is most valuable for high-dimensional problems where analytical integration is impossible. For simple problems like π, other methods are far more efficient — but the same logic scales to 1,000-dimensional financial models.

strategies.name: More samples → better estimate
strategies.outcome: The estimate converges toward π (3.14159...). With 100 samples: accurate to ~1 decimal place. With 10,000 samples: ~2 decimal places. With 1,000,000 samples: ~3 decimal places.
strategies.insight: Slow convergence is a fundamental property of random sampling — not a failure of the method. For most real-world applications, 3-4 significant figures is sufficient and easily achievable.

strategies.name: Examine variance of estimates across runs
strategies.outcome: Run the simulation multiple times with the same sample size. The spread of estimates gives you the standard error — a direct measure of how uncertain your estimate is.
strategies.insight: Monte Carlo is not just about point estimates — the variance across runs quantifies uncertainty. This is especially important in finance and risk management, where knowing the range of outcomes matters as much as the mean.

classroomObservations: Show the scatter plot of points coloured by inside/outside the circle. Watch the estimate converge as more points are added. Point out the oscillation — individual estimates bounce around even as they converge. This is the noise that 1/√n characterises. Ask: how would you use this logic to price a stock option? (Replace the circle with an option payoff function.)
realWorld: Derivative pricing (Black-Scholes can be solved analytically, but exotic options require Monte Carlo), value-at-risk (VaR) in risk management, drug clinical trial planning (sample size calculations), particle physics simulations, and climate model uncertainty quantification all use Monte Carlo methods.
tip: To estimate the uncertainty in your Monte Carlo estimate, run the simulation multiple times and compute the standard deviation of the estimates. The standard error is that standard deviation divided by √(number of runs). This tells you how confident to be in your answer.
furtherReading: Metropolis & Ulam (1949) — The Monte Carlo Method; Glasserman (2004) — Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering; Rubinstein & Kroese (2016) — Simulation and the Monte Carlo Method
numericalExample: True pi = 3.14159... With n=100 samples, estimate is accurate to ~1 decimal place (error ~0.1). n=10,000: ~2 decimal places (error ~0.01). n=1,000,000: ~3 decimal places (error ~0.001). To gain 1 extra decimal place, you need 100x more samples. This is the 1/sqrt(n) convergence rate — slow but guaranteed.

title: Conflict of Interest
subtitle: Agency Problems in Finance & Professional Services
concept: A conflict of interest arises when a person has private incentives that diverge from the duties they owe to someone else. In financial markets and professional services, advisers, analysts, auditors, and fund managers regularly face situations where their personal gain conflicts with their clients' best interests.
setup: Players act as financial advisers or professionals who make recommendations on behalf of clients. Unknown to the client, the adviser may have a financial interest in a particular recommendation (e.g. a higher commission, a referral fee, a shareholding). The game tests whether advisers act in clients' interests or their own, and whether clients can detect the bias.
keyInsight: Conflicts of interest are pervasive in finance and professional services — and difficult to eliminate because: (1) advisers always know more than clients (information asymmetry), and (2) monitoring is expensive. Disclosure is the legal minimum but does not eliminate the conflict and may actually make it worse (moral licensing).
lessons: The conflict arises from the combination of information asymmetry (the client doesn't know the adviser's private incentive) and the adviser's discretion (the adviser makes recommendations the client relies on).

Disclosure has a counterintuitive effect: studies show that once advisers disclose a conflict, they feel morally licensed to give more biased advice — as if disclosure has transferred the ethical responsibility to the client.

Structural solutions are more effective than disclosure: independence requirements (separating advice from product sales), fiduciary duties (legal obligation to act in the client's interest), and fee-only compensation (no commissions).
Reputation provides some constraint: advisers with long-term client relationships have more to lose from exploitation. Short-term or one-time transactions are more susceptible to conflicts.

strategies.name: Act in the client's best interest
strategies.outcome: The legally required and ethically correct outcome. May forgo personal gain but builds reputation and avoids legal liability. The outcome that well-designed incentive structures try to induce.
strategies.insight: Acting in the client's interest is rational when: (1) the relationship is long-term (reputation matters), (2) there is regulatory monitoring, or (3) professional norms are strong and internalised.

strategies.name: Exploit the conflict (self-deal)
strategies.outcome: Short-run gain for the adviser. Long-run costs: reputational damage if detected, regulatory sanctions, and personal liability. Social harm: clients receive suboptimal advice and market trust erodes.
strategies.insight: Self-dealing is rational in one-shot anonymous interactions with weak monitoring. This is why financial regulation focuses heavily on disclosure, licensing, and fiduciary duties.

strategies.name: Disclose the conflict transparently
strategies.outcome: The legal minimum. Allows clients to make informed decisions — in theory. In practice, clients often cannot evaluate complex conflicts and still defer to the adviser.
strategies.insight: Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient. Clients lack the expertise to adjust for disclosed conflicts. Structural separation (e.g. banning commission-based advice) is more effective.

classroomObservations: Ask students: did knowing about the conflict change how they interpreted the adviser's recommendation? Research shows it usually doesn't — clients continue to trust advisers even after disclosure. This is the real-world failure that justifies fiduciary rules beyond mere disclosure.
realWorld: Research analyst conflicts in investment banking (dot-com era: analysts rated stocks 'buy' while privately calling them 'dogs'), auditor conflicts (Big Four firms earn consulting fees from audit clients), insurance broker kickbacks (undisclosed commissions), credit rating agency conflicts (issuers pay for ratings), and pension adviser conflicts (fund managers paying for shelf space).
tip: The key question to ask of any recommendation: how does this adviser get paid? Fee structures reveal incentives. A commission-based adviser has an incentive to recommend high-commission products. A fee-only adviser earns the same regardless of what they recommend.
furtherReading: Jensen & Meckling (1976) — Theory of the Firm; Cain, Loewenstein & Moore (2005) — The Dirt on Coming Clean: Perverse Effects of Disclosing Conflicts of Interest; UK FCA (2012) — Retail Distribution Review (banned commission-based advice)

Even if Fund B has a 1% better annual return, the adviser earns $1,500 more recommending A. Over 10 years: client loses ~$13,000 in foregone returns (1%/yr compounded); adviser gains $15,000 in extra commissions. The conflict is financially significant.

title: Director Duties
subtitle: Corporate Governance & Fiduciary Obligations
concept: Corporate directors owe fiduciary duties to shareholders: primarily the duty of care (make decisions with due diligence and skill) and the duty of loyalty (act in shareholders' interests, not your own). These duties are enforced through legal liability and the Business Judgment Rule — which protects directors who act in good faith but not those who breach loyalty.
setup: Players act as directors of a corporation facing various governance decisions: approving transactions, overseeing management, handling related-party dealings, and responding to takeover bids. Each decision involves a trade-off between shareholder value, personal benefit, and legal compliance. Good governance decisions protect the company; poor ones expose directors to liability.
keyInsight: Good corporate governance reduces agency costs — the costs arising from the misalignment between managers' interests and shareholders' interests. Directors are the key institutional mechanism for ensuring managers act in shareholders' interests. When the board fails, the consequences (fraud, value destruction, regulatory action) are typically severe.
lessons: The Business Judgment Rule: courts give directors wide discretion for operational decisions, provided they are (1) adequately informed, (2) acting in good faith, and (3) free of personal conflict. All three conditions must be met — failing any one removes the protection.

The duty of loyalty is stricter than the duty of care: courts scrutinise related-party transactions, director compensation, and takeover decisions where directors have personal interests with particular scepticism. The burden of proof shifts to the director to show fairness.

Board independence is the structural solution to loyalty conflicts: independent directors (no employment or financial relationship with management) are better positioned to oversee management objectively. Post-Sarbanes-Oxley, US listed companies require independent audit, remuneration, and nomination committees.

The board's core governance functions: selecting and dismissing the CEO, setting executive pay, overseeing financial reporting, managing strategic risk, and protecting shareholder rights in M&A transactions.

strategies.name: Act in shareholders' best interest with proper process
strategies.outcome: Protected by the Business Judgment Rule. Decisions that turn out badly but were made with due process are not actionable. The rule encourages informed risk-taking without making directors liable for all bad outcomes.
strategies.insight: Good process is as important as good outcomes in corporate law. Document your deliberations, take independent advice, and disclose conflicts — these are defences, not formalities.

strategies.name: Approve a related-party transaction without scrutiny
strategies.outcome: Breach of the duty of loyalty if you have a personal interest in the transaction. Even if the transaction is at fair value, failure to follow proper approval procedures creates liability.
strategies.insight: Related-party transactions (contracts between the company and a director's other business interests) require full disclosure, independent board approval, and often shareholder vote. The process must be demonstrably fair.

strategies.name: Rubber-stamp management recommendations
strategies.outcome: Breach of the duty of care if directors fail to exercise independent judgment. 'Going along' with management on major decisions without proper scrutiny is a governance failure.
strategies.insight: The board's oversight function only has value if directors ask hard questions and push back. Passive boards are legal and reputational liabilities — as the Enron and Theranos cases demonstrated.

classroomObservations: Discuss the real cases: Smith v. Van Gorkom (director approved a merger over a phone call with no financial analysis — breached duty of care), In re Walt Disney (director compensation was approved but challenged — survived scrutiny because process was adequate). Ask: what separates a protected business judgment from a liability-creating governance failure?
realWorld: Enron (board waived conflict-of-interest policies for SPE transactions), WorldCom (audit committee failed to detect massive fraud), Theranos (board had no medical experts despite being a medical device company), and more recently, Silicon Valley Bank (board risk committee had no banking risk experience) — all examples of governance failures with catastrophic consequences.
tip: Directors are not expected to be perfect — they are expected to be diligent and loyal. The Business Judgment Rule is generous to directors who act in good faith with adequate information. But it provides no protection when personal interests conflict with shareholder interests and proper procedures are not followed.
furtherReading: Smith v. Van Gorkom (1985) — Delaware Supreme Court on duty of care; In re Caremark International (1996) — Director oversight duties; Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) — Post-Enron governance reforms; Cadbury Report (1992) — UK corporate governance code origins

Delaware Supreme Court: breach of duty of care — not because the price was wrong, but because the process was inadequate. Directors personally liable for $23.5m. The Business Judgment Rule requires adequate information, not perfect decisions.

title: Market Survival
subtitle: Competitive Dynamics, Cost Efficiency & Firm Exit
concept: In competitive markets, firms that cannot cover their costs exit, while efficient firms survive and potentially grow. Price competition drives prices toward cost, and economic profit tends toward zero in the long run. The market acts as a selection mechanism — rewarding efficiency and penalising waste.
setup: You manage a firm competing in a market with multiple rivals. Each period you set prices or choose output, incur costs, and earn revenues. If your revenues fall below your costs persistently, you exit the market. New entrants appear when profits attract them. Your goal is to survive and maximise cumulative profits over the game.
keyInsight: Long-run competitive equilibrium is zero economic profit — not zero accounting profit. All costs must be covered, including the opportunity cost of capital. Firms that earn above-normal profits attract entry; firms that incur losses exit. The market reaches equilibrium when price equals the minimum of the average total cost curve.
lessons: Short-run vs. long-run equilibrium: in the short run, firms can earn profits or losses (capacity and entry are fixed). In the long run, entry and exit drive economic profits to zero. The long-run equilibrium price is the minimum average total cost.

Fixed vs. variable costs matter for exit decisions: in the short run, a firm should continue operating as long as price exceeds average variable cost (contribution to fixed costs). In the long run, all costs are variable — exit if price < average total cost.

Efficiency and survival: firms with lower costs survive longer and can price more aggressively. Cost advantages can come from scale economies, better technology, lower input costs, or superior organisation.

Dynamic competition: the market is never in static equilibrium. Firms invest in cost reduction, product innovation, and market expansion. The survival of the fittest is a selection process, not a static outcome.

strategies.name: Price competitively and control costs
strategies.outcome: Survive by matching market prices while keeping costs below revenue. Efficiency is the sustainable competitive advantage in a market with competitive entry.
strategies.insight: Cost leadership: being the lowest-cost producer allows you to price at market rates and earn positive margin. It also allows aggressive price-cutting when necessary to defend market share.

strategies.name: Price above market to protect margin
strategies.outcome: Lose market share to lower-priced rivals. Sustainable only if your product has genuine differentiation that customers value enough to pay the premium.
strategies.insight: Premium pricing requires differentiation. Without it, pricing above market is a recipe for exit. The choice between cost leadership and differentiation is Porter's fundamental strategic trade-off.

strategies.name: Invest in cost reduction
strategies.outcome: Short-run sacrifice of profit for long-run competitive advantage. Firms that invest in efficiency improvements can survive market downturns that drive out higher-cost rivals.
strategies.insight: Long-run survival requires reinvestment. Standing still while rivals improve is equivalent to falling behind. This is why competitive markets drive productivity growth.

classroomObservations: Show which firms survived and which exited. Ask: what distinguished survivors from exiters? Was it pricing strategy, cost structure, or luck? This connects to the empirical finding that the most productive firms grow and the least productive exit — markets perform selection, not just allocation.
realWorld: Retail (Amazon drove out Borders, Circuit City, Toys R Us — all failed to match Amazon's cost structure), airlines (low-cost carriers Ryanair and easyJet drove out legacy carriers on short-haul routes), and manufacturing (Chinese entry into textiles eliminated many Western producers) all illustrate market selection at work.
tip: Track your costs per unit as carefully as your revenues. Firms often fail not because of pricing mistakes but because of cost structures that looked sustainable at higher volumes. Fixed costs become fatal when volumes fall.
furtherReading: Alchian (1950) — Uncertainty, Evolution and Economic Theory; Porter (1980) — Competitive Strategy; Hopenhayn (1992) — Entry, Exit, and Firm Dynamics in Long Run Equilibrium
numericalExample: Firm A: price=$20, unit cost=$15, contribution=$5. Fixed costs=$1,000/month. Break-even volume = 1,000/5 = 200 units. If demand falls to 150 units: revenue=$3,000, variable cost=$2,250, contribution=$750, loss=$250/month. Short-run: stay open (contribution >0). Long-run: exit if no improvement (can't cover fixed costs). This is the shutdown rule in practice.

title: A/B Testing
subtitle: Multiplayer Experiment Simulation: Variant Choice, Timing & Profit
concept: A/B testing is a repeated decision system, not a one-time statistics quiz. Teams choose between two variants, decide how long to run tests, and then face delayed sales outcomes with noise. Good teams balance speed and evidence quality so they ship profitable changes while avoiding false winners.
setup: Two teams compete across 5-6 rounds. In each round, each team selects between two options (Variant A or Variant B), sets traffic split and test duration, then submits. A clearly visible progression control is used to move time: 'Advance 1 Day' and 'Advance 5 Days'. After advancing time, the round reveals sales impact (increase, decrease, or no meaningful change), confidence quality, and profit effect. Teams decide whether to ship, hold, or rerun. Final ranking is cumulative profit.
keyInsight: The fastest team does not always win, and the most cautious team can miss profitable opportunities. Winning requires good test discipline: enough evidence to avoid false positives, but not so much delay that opportunity cost destroys value.
lessons: Test duration is a strategic choice. Short windows are faster but noisier; longer windows reduce uncertainty but can delay gains.
A sales uplift is not enough by itself. Teams should evaluate incremental profit after implementation cost and discount effects.
False positives are expensive. Shipping a bad variant can reduce profit for multiple future rounds.
Sequential adaptation matters. Teams should update decisions from prior rounds rather than repeating fixed rules.

strategies.name: Fast iteration strategy
strategies.outcome: Uses more 'Advance 1 Day' cycles to make rapid decisions and capture early upside.
strategies.insight: Can outperform when effects are large, but risks overreacting to noise and shipping weak variants.

strategies.name: Evidence-first strategy
strategies.outcome: Uses more 'Advance 5 Days' windows for stronger signal quality before shipping.
strategies.insight: Reduces false-positive risk, but may lose profit due to slower rollout when true uplift exists.

strategies.name: Hybrid strategy
strategies.outcome: Starts with fast checks, then extends duration only for borderline tests.
strategies.insight: Often gives the best profit-risk balance by combining speed with selective rigor.

classroomObservations: Show a per-round board with each team's variant choice, time-advance path (1 day vs 5 days), observed lift, and realized profit. Students quickly see that the same variant can look good on day 1 and weak by day 5, and that decision quality drives final profit more than headline conversion alone.
realWorld: Product teams at major digital firms run experimentation programs with explicit tradeoffs between speed and certainty. The operational challenge is deciding when evidence is sufficient to ship, while controlling false positives and protecting long-run margin.
tip: Use round scoring like: ProfitImpact = IncrementalRevenue - RolloutCost - BadShipPenalty. Rank teams by cumulative profit; use decision accuracy as a tie-breaker. Place 'Advance 1 Day' and 'Advance 5 Days' buttons near the decision panel so progression is obvious.
furtherReading: Fisher (1935) - The Design of Experiments; Kohavi, Tang & Xu (2020) - Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments; Deng et al. (2016) - Continuous Monitoring of A/B Tests
numericalExample: Variant A: 5% conversion (baseline). Variant B: 6.5% conversion. Observed lift = +1.5pp. With n=1,000/group: Z = 1.56, p = 0.12 — not significant. With n=3,800/group: Z = 2.0, p = 0.046 — significant at 5%. Running too early gives a false positive ~30% of the time instead of 5%. The cost: shipping a bad variant that cuts profit for multiple rounds.

title: Customer Churn
subtitle: Multiplayer Retention Simulation: Risk Rules, Intervention & ROI
concept: Customer churn management is a repeated targeting problem under uncertainty. Teams read customer behavior data, define risk patterns (for example: inactivity, low session depth, falling usage, poor NPS), and decide who should receive retention effort. Good churn strategy balances recall, precision, and intervention cost rather than maximizing outreach volume.
setup: Two teams compete across 5-6 rounds. Each round starts with a fresh customer panel showing features such as days inactive, average sessions/week, spend trend, support tickets, tenure, and NPS. Teams submit threshold rules to classify high-risk customers (for example: inactive > X days and avg sessions < Y) and choose intervention mix (sales call, discount, onboarding support, service recovery). The simulator then reveals true churners, customers saved, false positives, and intervention cost. Winner is based on cumulative Net Retained Value, not raw saves.
keyInsight: Saving the most customers is not always the best strategy. If a team flags too many low-risk customers, intervention spend rises and ROI collapses. Strong performance comes from identifying truly at-risk valuable customers and matching them with cost-effective interventions.
lessons: Rule design is a precision-recall tradeoff. Lower thresholds catch more churners but increase false positives and sales workload.
Risk should be value-weighted. Saving a high-CLV account is usually worth more than saving multiple low-value accounts.
Intervention choice matters as much as detection. Discounts can improve short-run saves but may erode margin and train discount-seeking behavior.
Model drift is realistic. Patterns that worked in one round can weaken when market conditions or customer behavior shift.

strategies.name: High-precision targeting
strategies.outcome: Targets fewer customers, yields lower outreach cost, and usually strong ROI. Risk: some true churners are missed.
strategies.insight: Best when intervention capacity is limited and false-positive cost is high.

strategies.name: High-recall targeting
strategies.outcome: Catches more true churners and can boost gross saves. Risk: high false positives can make the program unprofitable.
strategies.insight: Useful when churn shock risk is high, but only with strict budget control.

strategies.name: Segmented intervention strategy
strategies.outcome: Uses different actions by risk/type (for example, onboarding for low-usage new users, service recovery for dissatisfied users, selective discount for price-sensitive users).
strategies.insight: Usually delivers the best Net Retained Value because treatment cost is matched to likely response.

classroomObservations: Show per-round confusion metrics (TP, FP, FN), customers saved, and profit impact. Students quickly learn that the team with the highest save count can still lose if targeting is noisy or intervention spend is excessive. Debrief threshold changes round-by-round and how teams adapted to pattern drift.
realWorld: Telecom, SaaS, streaming, and banking retention teams all run this loop in production: risk scoring, queue prioritization, treatment assignment, and measured save uplift against cost. Mature teams optimize for retained value and margin impact, not just churn-rate optics.
tip: Use this score each round: Net Retained Value = SavedValue - InterventionCost - FalsePositiveCost. Track precision (TP/(TP+FP)) and recall (TP/(TP+FN)) alongside ROI. Final winner should be cumulative Net Retained Value, with precision as tie-breaker.
furtherReading: Fader & Hardie (2005) - A Note on Deriving the Pareto/NBD Model and Related Expressions; Gupta et al. (2006) - Modeling Customer Lifetime Value; Verbeke et al. (2012) - New Insights into Churn Prediction in the Telecommunication Sector
numericalExample: 100 at-risk customers, CLV=$1,200 each. Intervention cost=$50/customer. True churners=30, non-churners=70. If you target all 100: save 30 x $1,200 = $36,000 revenue, spend $5,000 on intervention. Net = $31,000. If you use a precision model and target only 40 (30 true + 10 false positives): save same 30 x $1,200, spend only $2,000. Net = $34,000 — $3,000 better. Precision matters.

title: Market Basket Analysis
subtitle: Multiplayer Retail Simulation: Pairing, Margin & Competitive Response
concept: Market basket analysis is strongest when used in a repeated decision game, not as a one-shot quiz. Teams use support, confidence, and lift to choose pair promotions in a shared market where both sides compete for the same demand. The winner is the team that turns basket intelligence into cumulative profit under constraints.
setup: Two teams compete across 6 rounds (weeks). Each round, each team secretly selects one product pair to promote and one intensity (low, medium, high). Choices are revealed simultaneously. Demand updates from pair lift, promo intensity, and rivalry effects (if both teams target overlapping baskets, uplift is diluted). Teams then receive revenue, pay COGS and promo spend, and absorb stockout or markdown penalties. Final ranking is cumulative profit, with revenue as tie-breaker.
keyInsight: There is no always-best pair. The best move depends on margin, inventory, and the opponent's current choice. A high-lift pair can still be a bad strategy when promo costs are high, inventory is tight, or both teams collide on the same segment.
lessons: Support still matters: low-support pairs can look strong in one round but are unstable and create higher forecast error.
Lift is directional, not the objective. Teams must combine association strength with unit margin, promo cost, and inventory limits.
Competition changes payoffs. If both teams choose overlapping pairs, each side's incremental uplift is reduced.
Delayed effects matter. Repeated deep discounting can grow short-run volume but weaken later-round margin quality.

strategies.name: Balanced portfolio strategy
strategies.outcome: Mix high-margin moderate-lift pairs with occasional high-lift volume plays. This usually produces steadier cumulative profit.
strategies.insight: Winning the game is about risk-adjusted consistency, not just one big round.

strategies.name: Opponent-aware counter strategy
strategies.outcome: Track rival picks and avoid direct overlap when collision penalties are high; redirect to under-contested segments.
strategies.insight: A second-best pair in isolation can be best-in-round after accounting for competitive dilution.

strategies.name: High-intensity push strategy
strategies.outcome: Can win single rounds on volume but becomes expensive if repeated and often triggers stockout or markdown penalties.
strategies.insight: Use high intensity as a tactical move when inventory is deep and overlap risk is low.

classroomObservations: Use a round log that shows both teams' pair choices, intensity, and profit decomposition (revenue, COGS, promo cost, penalties). Students quickly see that highest revenue can still lose on profit, and that repeated overlap destroys value for both sides.
realWorld: Retailers use basket intelligence inside weekly competitive loops, not static reports: grocery bundles, e-commerce cross-sell slots, and quick-service combo campaigns are all adjusted against rival promotions and stock constraints.
tip: Start with this model: UnitsSold = BaseDemand * PairLift * PromoMultiplier * CompetitionFactor * RandomShock. Profit = Revenue - COGS - PromoCost - StockoutPenalty - MarkdownPenalty. Keep cumulative profit as the primary win metric.
furtherReading: Agrawal & Srikant (1994) - Fast Algorithms for Mining Association Rules; Han, Pei & Yin (2000) - Mining Frequent Patterns Without Candidate Generation; Linden, Smith & York (2003) - Amazon.com Recommendations: Item-to-Item Collaborative Filtering
numericalExample: 10,000 transactions. {Beer, Diapers} appear together 500 times: support=5%. Beer alone=2,000 times, diapers alone=1,000. Confidence(Beer->Diapers)=500/2000=25%. Baseline rate of diapers=10%. Lift=25%/10%=2.5. This means beer buyers buy diapers 2.5x more than average — a strong, actionable association. Place them near each other or cross-sell.

title: The Signal
subtitle: Social Proof, Information Cascades & Conformity Bias
concept: When individuals don't know the truth, they often use others' beliefs as a signal. This 'social proof' can aggregate genuine information — but it can also cascade false beliefs through a group, producing confident collective errors.
setup: Each round, players rate their confidence (0–100) that an economic statement is true. Before submitting, they see a social proof cue: '72% of people agree' or '18% of people agree'. Unknown to players, these percentages are randomly varied: roughly half the room sees a low figure (~15–30%) and half sees a high figure (~70–85%). After all rounds, the class compares the two groups' average confidence.
keyInsight: If social proof systematically shifts confidence — independently of the statement's actual truth — that is conformity bias at work. A statement rated 65/100 by the high-proof group but 38/100 by the low-proof group has been distorted by the signal, not by evidence.
lessons: Social proof is a genuine heuristic shortcut that can be both adaptive and dangerous.
Information cascades can cause rational individuals to ignore their private signals, creating collective errors (Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer & Welch 1992).
The Asch conformity experiments showed ~75% of subjects gave an obviously wrong answer at least once when confederates did so.
Financial bubbles, viral misinformation, and bank runs all share a common structure: people update on what others are doing rather than on fundamentals.
Diversity of independent signals is more informative than a large sample of correlated (socially influenced) signals.
strategies: Anchoring independently: commit to your private assessment before looking at what others believe.
Source evaluation: ask whether the 'crowd' had access to independent information or was itself influenced.
Contrarian awareness: the value of a dissenting opinion rises as the majority grows larger.
Calibration: well-calibrated confidence tracks accuracy — overconfidence and underconfidence both have costs.
classroomObservations: Groups shown high social proof typically rate statements 10–25 points higher on average than the low group — even for false statements.
The effect is usually larger for genuinely ambiguous statements (those students find hard to evaluate independently).
After the reveal, students are often surprised they were manipulated — this visceral reaction reinforces the concept.
Asking students to discuss which statements shifted them the most surfaces rich peer discussion about epistemic confidence.
realWorld: The mechanism behind The Signal underlies social media virality (likes/shares as social proof), asset price bubbles (rising prices as 'proof' of value), preference falsification in authoritarian states, and jury deliberation dynamics. Cialdini's 'Influence' (1984) catalogued social proof as one of the six fundamental principles of persuasion.
tip: After the debrief, ask: 'What would have made you more resistant to the social proof cue?' Common answers — more domain knowledge, more time to think, explicit awareness of the manipulation — surface actionable insights for real life.

The 27-point gap is pure social signal — the truth value of the statement was identical for both groups. Even more striking: both groups averaged above 50, meaning a majority in both groups leaned toward the wrong answer.

title: Crypto Bubble
subtitle: Asset Bubbles, Minsky Moments & Algorithmic Contagion
concept: Asset bubbles form when prices persistently exceed fundamental value — driven by momentum, extrapolative expectations, and FOMO. Minsky's financial instability hypothesis argues that stability itself breeds risk-taking: prolonged booms lead to increasingly fragile positions that collapse suddenly when confidence breaks.
setup: Students trade tokens in a live double-sided order book. Each token pays a $10 dividend per period, so its fundamental value equals remaining periods × $10 (declining each round). Three algorithmic traders (Algo A/B/C) are always present, buying aggressively in early periods and panic-selling when the instructor fires the Minsky Moment shock. Students post bids and asks; trades execute whenever best bid ≥ best ask.
keyInsight: Even rational students often drive prices above fundamental value — because buying above FV is individually rational if you expect to sell at an even higher price to the next buyer (the 'Greater Fool'). The Minsky Moment shows what happens when the chain of greater fools runs out: prices collapse faster than they rose, and leveraged positions are destroyed.
lessons: Fundamental value is objectively calculable — yet markets routinely ignore it
Bubble dynamics require only a subset of optimistic buyers; rational traders can be swept along
Algorithmic traders can amplify both the boom (momentum buying) and the bust (panic liquidation)
Liquidity disappears exactly when it is most needed — bids vanish as crash unfolds
Post-bubble price recovery is slower than the crash — asymmetric volatility
strategies: Track the fundamental value line — any price above it is a pure speculation premium
Sell into strength: if others are still buying bullishly, that is your exit window
Watch the order book depth — thin bids signal fragility even if the last trade was high
Algo Traders reveal where the bots are: if they dominate bids, the bubble has bot support; when they flip to asks, the crash has begun
After the Minsky shock, consider aggressive asks — other human players may still be in denial
classroomObservations: Most sessions produce a clear bubble 30–60% above FV in periods 2–5 before the shock
Post-shock crashes often overshoot — prices fall below FV as panic sets in
Students who sold early often regret it mid-bubble; those who held late regret it most
Watching bots panic-sell makes the Minsky concept visceral and memorable
Debrief: ask who held, who sold into strength, who tried to buy the dip — maps directly to investor archetypes
realWorld: The 2017 Bitcoin rally (from ~$1K to $20K and back to $3K), the dot-com boom, 2008 mortgage securities, and 2021 meme stocks all exhibit the same structure: prices divorced from fundamentals, momentum-driven buying, sudden collapse when sentiment reverses. Hyman Minsky predicted this pattern 30 years before it became mainstream.
tip: Fire the Minsky Moment mid-bubble for maximum impact — ideally around period 5–6 when prices are furthest above FV. Warn students beforehand that 'something may happen at any time' to keep them alert.

title: Xero Reconciliation
subtitle: Solo Simulation: Bank Reconciliation, Duplicate Detection & GST Return
concept: Bank reconciliation is the process of matching a business's internal accounting records against its bank statement. In practice this means categorising transactions, spotting errors like duplicates, and ensuring the GST return reflects only legitimate transactions. In New Zealand, GST-registered businesses must file returns showing GST collected on sales minus GST paid on purchases — the net amount goes to or from IRD.
setup: Students work solo through three randomised NZ business scenarios (café, IT consulting, retail). Each scenario has three phases: (1) categorise bank transactions into Revenue, Cost of Sales, Expense, or Wages; (2) identify which transaction is a duplicate; (3) complete a simplified GST return by calculating GST on sales and GST on purchases. The game uses a Xero-inspired interface to mirror real-world accounting software.
keyInsight: Reconciliation is not just tidying up — it is the control that catches errors before they affect tax obligations, financial statements, and business decisions. A single duplicate transaction can simultaneously overstate expenses, understate profit, and incorrectly claim GST input credits.
lessons: Categorising transactions correctly is the foundation of both management accounts and tax compliance. Revenue, Cost of Sales, Expenses, and Wages each affect profit differently.
Duplicate transactions are the most common bank reconciliation error. They arise from double-entry by suppliers, bank re-processing, or manual data entry mistakes.
GST in New Zealand is 15%. Businesses collect GST on sales and claim it back on purchases. Net GST payable = GST on sales minus GST on purchases.
Wages are not subject to GST — a common point of confusion. PAYE (income tax withheld) is separate from the GST system entirely.
Monthly reconciliation prevents errors from compounding across multiple GST return periods.

strategies.name: Systematic categorisation
strategies.outcome: Assign all transactions before reviewing any — then check your work as a set.
strategies.insight: Processing transactions in batch reduces context-switching errors and makes patterns (like duplicates) more visible.

strategies.name: Duplicate detection heuristic
strategies.outcome: Look for identical descriptions and amounts on different dates — especially with suppliers who invoice regularly.
strategies.insight: Duplicates rarely appear on the same date. A second identical charge days later is the most common pattern.

strategies.name: GST reconciliation check
strategies.outcome: Verify: GST on sales = total revenue × 3/23 (or amount ÷ 1.15 × 0.15). GST on purchases = same formula applied to GST-bearing expenses.
strategies.insight: If your calculated net GST seems unusually high or low, check whether a wage or exempt item was incorrectly included.

classroomObservations: Students often struggle most with wages (no GST) and with spotting duplicates when descriptions are nearly identical. Debrief by showing what the P&L and GST return would look like with and without the duplicate — the downstream effect makes the stakes concrete.
realWorld: In New Zealand, GST-registered businesses with turnover over $60,000 must file GST returns (typically every two months). Errors in reconciliation flow directly into incorrect GST returns, which can trigger IRD audits and interest charges. Xero is the dominant accounting platform for NZ SMEs and automates much of the matching — but humans still need to review and approve categorisations.
tip: After the game, show students the actual NZ GST return form (IR3B) and walk through how the numbers from this simulation map to each box. Box 5 (total sales incl. GST), Box 13 (GST on sales), Box 11 (total purchases incl. GST), Box 15 (GST on purchases), Box 20 (net GST).

GST → GST on purchases = $5,428 ÷ 1.15 × 0.15 = $708. Net GST payable to IRD = $1,950 − $708 = $1,242. If the duplicate $2,300 charge had not been caught, GST on purchases would have been $708 + $300 = $1,008 — overstating the claim by $300.

title: Capital Structure Lab
subtitle: Debt, Equity, WACC, and Value Creation
concept: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity a firm uses to finance projects. Debt is usually cheaper but increases financial risk. Equity is safer for solvency but more expensive and dilutive. The central decision is whether project returns exceed the firm's weighted average cost of capital (WACC).
setup: You run a company for four rounds. Each round you choose one project and decide its funding split across internal cash, debt, and equity. The simulation calculates WACC, realized returns, leverage, and credit rating updates automatically.
keyInsight: A project creates value only when return exceeds cost of capital. Funding choices change that cost. More debt can lift returns at first, then backfire as risk and borrowing cost rise.
lessons: Debt is often the cheapest source of capital, but not at high leverage.
Equity reduces default pressure but raises the hurdle rate and dilutes ownership.
WACC is not static; it changes as leverage and credit rating evolve.
High-return projects can still destroy value when financing cost is mismanaged.
Good finance strategy balances upside, resilience, and future flexibility.

strategies.name: Balanced Funding
strategies.outcome: Uses a mix of internal cash, moderate debt, and selective equity to keep WACC controlled.
strategies.insight: Usually strongest for consistent value creation over multiple rounds.

strategies.name: Aggressive Leverage
strategies.outcome: Boosts near-term debt funding and can look attractive early.
strategies.insight: Often triggers rating pressure and rising debt cost in later rounds.

strategies.name: Overly Conservative
strategies.outcome: Avoids debt almost entirely and leans heavily on equity/internal cash.
strategies.insight: Stable but may miss positive-NPV opportunities because the effective hurdle stays high.

classroomObservations: Students typically understand debt vs equity much faster when they see credit rating and WACC move after their own choices. Debrief by asking when their leverage shifted from helpful to harmful.
realWorld: The same logic appears in corporate treasury, infrastructure finance, private equity capital stacks, and startup financing rounds.
tip: Before locking a round, compare expected project return against current WACC and ask how this funding mix changes next-round flexibility.
numericalExample: If a $300,000 project realizes 14% and current WACC is 9%, value created is roughly $15,000. If WACC rises to 13% because leverage became too high, the same realized return creates only about $3,000.
